title: Trio Help 50000 Deaf Persons Sit for Govt Exams & Become Job-Ready With Skill Training
content: Originally reported and written in August 2023, this story has been republished as part of our archival content. Indian Sign Language (ISL) was the first language Nita Gopalakrishnan learnt. English was second. Born to deaf parents but being able to hear perfectly well herself shaped Nita’s formative years, and changed her perspective of the world, as she saw it through her parents’ eyes. In 2020, the 42-year-old founded Yunikee — a Hyderabad-based organisation dedicated to helping persons with hearing disabilities in India — with her husband Chaithanya Kothapalli (44) and her colleague Rahul Jain (34). “I never saw my parents as being different from other parents,” Nita shares. “To me, it was just a matter of my parents not being able to hear.” Being a special educator, Nita realised the inaccessibility of resources that deaf children often faced, a realisation that later served as her driving force to co-found Yunikee. For Chaithanya, an IT professional, it was watching his wife Nita’s work ethic while she taught deaf kids, which had a profound impact on him. So, after a 25-year-long stint in the corporate world, Chaithanya quit his job in 2020 to join Nita in creating the social impact platform. Joining their vision was Rahul, an ISL teacher who had been working with Nita since 2017 teaching deaf kids in special schools. Being deaf, Rahul brought unique insights to the table on how they could formulate a platform that would cater to solving some vital problems that the community was experiencing. Yunikee caters to thousands of deaf young adults through campaigns, programs and activities that teach ISL (Indian Sign Language), Picture source: Chaithanya A conversation sparks an idea It is not every day that three people from very different walks of life bond over an idea. As Chaithanya, Nita and Rahul share the story of Yunikee’s inception, they are well aware of the incredible alignment of thoughts, among other things. “It was thanks to the COVID-19 pandemic,” says Chaithanya. The trio was discussing the unfairness of the situation — how abled students had the privilege of continuing their schooling online while students with hearing disabilities were denied this basic right. They figured that this discrimination extended beyond the classroom. “What if we were to start a platform that enabled hearing disabled people to access equal opportunities in terms of jobs, skillset training and more?” they thought. “That’s where it all started,” Chaithanya shares. And there was no looking back. “Yunikee is an actual word (in Telugu) that translates to ‘I exist. Don’t ignore me.’” The reason for this stark reminder is that, unlike people of other disabilities, deaf persons cannot be identified unless one speaks to them, says Chaithanya. He continues, “Through Yunikee, we wanted to bring an identity to them.” As the trio dived deeper into the project, the most enthusiastic of them was Rahul. From personal experiences, Rahul’s views were cemented in the fact that the people of his community were not given the right tools that they needed to excel. He shares that there were “close to no learning platforms for deaf people at all”. Yunikee, he says, addresses this gap by empowering deaf adults to free themselves from the chokehold of dependency. “We are simply forced to continue our family business because of a lack of options in the job market. As someone who would scour the job market looking for jobs, and now as someone who is part of an initiative that trains deaf people to be adept at what they do, I have seen both ends of the spectrum,” Rahul says. “Yunikee enables us to be independent.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Yunikee (@yunikee4deaf) Championing change through campaigns Yunikee has extended its services to over “50,000 deaf persons” across India through the wide gamut of activities, projects and campaigns that it conducts. Take, for instance, the ‘Sign Medium’. Over “10,000 deaf adolescents” have been taught sign language through this programme, which started in 2020. Chaithanya recalls, “We ran a social media campaign inviting those interested in learning ISL to register.” The response from this initiative was so overwhelming that Yunikee now conducts over 120 different courses such as stock trading, web development, IELTS and more for their participants today. Dibyendu, along with his parents, was part of one of these workshops conducted by Nita last year. “It was a very nice experience to learn sign language and be able to communicate freely. Earlier, I was only able to do some gestures and was not able to express myself freely. Now I can communicate with my family and deaf friends,” he shares. The 25-year-old is now working in the web development sector and is extremely happy with his prospects. What sets Yunikee apart is that the impact is multi-faceted, extending beyond a single participant. For instance, their ‘Champions League’ programme helps deaf people looking to start ventures of their own. By assisting them with workshops in sign language, completing legal formalities, and chartered accountancy services, the team ensures that they are well-equipped with everything they need to know before starting their business. The team at Yunikee comprises 40 deaf adults who bring their individual experiences to formulate programs, Picture source: Chaithanya The first cohort of the Champions League programme is ongoing, and Chaithanya shares that of the nine business ventures so far, three startups are already up and running. One of them is ‘Sign Skill Bridge’ founded by Vishnu Prasath from Madurai, Tamil Nadu. Sharing how the business incubation programme helped him, he says he owes it to the networking he was able to do in the past three months. “I have been learning a lot. Following step-by-step instructions, I successfully set up the ‘Sign Skill Bridge’ as a centre.” Encouraging others to also avail of it, Vishnu says that “the programme covers various courses that have made start-up and business establishment accessible for the deaf community entrepreneurs for the first time in India”. He adds that he is excited to see how it unfolds. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Yunikee (@yunikee4deaf) Though Vishnu had the idea for ‘Sign Skill Bridge’ for years, he never had the confidence to share it with the world due to communication barriers. But in 2022, a meeting with Yunikee opened him up to the world of possibilities. Today his learning centre empowers over 150 deaf persons with its inclusive classroom where courses such as web development, 3D painting, graphic designing and more are taught. Vishnu’s story reminds Chaithanya of the tremendous impact Yunikee has had on the people they have worked with. “Every time I doubt if we are on the right path, I think of Vishnu’s story and see it as a reminder to keep going.” Preparing for life – and more Yunikee helps deaf adults get opportunities for jobs, setting up their own businesses, taking government exams and more, Picture source: Chaithanya A unique aspect of Yunikee’s work is the partnerships they conduct. One such project in 2022 trained 10 deaf girls in Pakistan in hairdressing and applying makeup. These girls then went on to set up their individual parlours, says Nita. While enabling deaf persons to access mainstream jobs is one pillar, the other is enabling them to access what is duly theirs. Yunikee has successfully trained over 140 deaf people to appear for government exams, out of which, 40 of them have secured jobs. “Despite there being a one percent reservation in government sectors for deaf people, these positions often go vacant as the candidates are unable to clear the exams,” Nita explains. “That’s where we come in.” Anil Mishra, who took the course last year on banking using sign language, is now working at a bank in Ahmedabad. He says the nine months he spent learning were worth it and helped him clear the IBPS exam. “While there was always a one percent reservation for deaf people in banks, we had no support in learning and preparing for the exams.” He gives the success of his credit to Sagar, who is one of the 40 team members at Yunikee who teach, mentor and formulate these programs. “Sagar sir taught us all the topics in detail enabling me to confidently take the exam which led to my selection.” Nita shares that apart from her and Chaithanya, the team of 40 comprises deaf adults, each of whom brings in their own expertise and individual insights that contribute to making the platform a holistic learning space. “Being deaf themselves, they have lived experiences and have an understanding of what is needed,” she says. As the trio recounts several gratifying moments through Yunikee’s journey, their stories are tinged with a deep sense of satisfaction as well as a need for advocacy. “There are still miles to go,” says Nita, echoing the thoughts of the other two. Edited by Padmashree Pande

title: Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance
content: Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 12:42 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Halito akana (Hello friends), Indigenous governance models, practiced for millennia and rooted in our cosmovisions, traditions, laws, and cultural values, are systems of cultural sovereignty through which our Peoples enact self-determination and ensure balanced relationships within communities and with our more-than-human-relatives in the lands and waters we call home. Our traditional models of governance often center collective decision-making, community responsibility, and respect for ancestral knowledge, which is intertwined with the natural laws of Mother Earth. By maintaining self-governance, Indigenous communities protect their cultural identity, strengthen local leadership, and address social, economic, and environmental issues in ways that reflect their Peoples’ values, needs, and perspectives. International bodies like the United Nations recognize the effectiveness and global importance of Indigenous governance in managing land, water, and biodiversity, improving well being, and addressing inequities, and the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples affirms rights to self-determination and self-government. In this issue of the CSQ, we share examples of cultural sovereignty in practice from the regions where we work. Some lessons that arise include: Indigenous governance systems have endured for centuries, surviving colonialism, State pressures, and modern challenges. They are living systems rooted in ancestral knowledge and adaptable to community needs. Leadership is based on service to the community, not personal power. Authority is earned through demonstrated responsibility, wisdom, and integrity. Decision-making is collective. Governance is inseparable from stewardship of land, water, plants, and animals. The land and all beings, flows, and entities are seen as living relatives with whom we have reciprocal relationships and responsibilities to protect. They are not treated merely as resources. Political, spiritual, and cultural life are intertwined. Elders and knowledge keepers guide decisions and maintain traditions. Women and youth are recognized as vital to governance, carrying knowledge of food systems, environmental stewardship, cultural continuity, and more. Indigenous governance systems face ongoing threats from State policies, extractive industries, and legal frameworks that often undermine autonomy. Recognition of Indigenous governance by States is often partial or conditional, leading to tensions and manufactured dependency. Despite these pressures, communities continue to assert their rights, resist dispossession, and adapt their governance to new realities. Indigenous governance is not static, but incorporates new tools, technologies, and organizational forms to address modern challenges such as climate change and legal advocacy. The most important message is perhaps one that Irma Velásquez Nimatuj (Maya K’iche’) points out: “The challenge, according to those consulted in the regions where Cultural Survival operates, is not proving that Indigenous self-governance works, but rather getting nation States to stop sabotaging it.” Our systems have governed our Peoples from the beginning. Our greatest challenges are the outside threats that hinder our self-determination. As a supporter of Cultural Survival, you contribute to the efforts of Indigenous Peoples who are safeguarding knowledge systems, languages, and lifeways for future generations. Please give generously at www.cs.org/donate. Hóchi yakoke li hoke (I thank you all so much), Aimee Roberson (Choctaw and Chickasaw), Executive Director Main Image

title: How Indigenous Protected Areas became a vital way to protect nature in Australia
content:
When you think of conservation in Australia, chances are you'll think of a national park.
But there's another fast-growing way of conserving land: Indigenous Protected Areas (IPAs). These areas of land or sea Country are voluntarily dedicated by Traditional Owners to protect nature and cultural values and responsibilities.
Once dedicated, an IPA becomes part of Australia's National Reserve System—our network of protected areas. To protect the area, Indigenous rangers tackle invasive species and undertake cultural burning and many other tasks.
In 2022, the Australian government signed up to an international pledge to protect 30% of lands and waters by 2030. This is one reason why IPAs have grown so rapidly in recent years.
In July, 4.7 million hectares (11.6 million acres) of the Simpson Desert was dedicated as the newest protected area—the Pmere Atherre Antenterreme IPA.
Maintaining the success of Indigenous Protected Areas will require long-term funding, strong Indigenous governance and complementary conservation elsewhere.
How does this work?
While national parks are established and managed by governments, IPAs are Indigenous-led.
After deciding to establish an IPA, Traditional Owners develop a management plan and determine how Country is to be cared for, drawing on Indigenous knowledge and contemporary conservation science.
Caring for Country means looking after plants, animals, water, fire, sacred places and cultural practices as part of an interconnected whole.
Declaring an IPA doesn't change existing tenure arrangements. For example, an IPA can cover freehold Indigenous land, land granted under land-rights legislation, Indigenous-held leasehold or pastoral land, Crown land and marine areas.
From pilot program to over half of Australia's reserve system
In 1998, Nantawarrina became Australia's first Indigenous Protected Area. The former pastoral station in South Australia's Flinders Ranges was heavily degraded. Over the following decades, the Nipapanha people worked to restore the land and its biodiversity.
There are now 96 IPAs across Australia, spanning 113 million hectares (279 million acres). That's almost 15% of the continent. Marine IPAs cover a smaller portion of Australian waters—9.3 million hectares (23 million acres), or about 1.1% of our marine estate.
The growth of IPAs has far outstripped the growth of other types of conservation land. IPAs now make up more than 55% of lands protected in Australia's National Reserve System.
Across all types of protection—both government and non-government—25% of Australia's land is now protected, and 24% of seas are highly protected "no-take" areas where fishing is banned.
The largest IPAs lie in Australia's deserts, some of the world's largest uncleared arid ecosystems. They form part of a vast, culturally connected landscape shaped by Indigenous stewardship over tens of thousands of years.
People who care for Country
At the heart of Indigenous Protected Areas are Indigenous rangers, who combine cultural practice and traditional knowledge with contemporary conservation practices.
Ranger teams began growing in number from 2007, when dedicated federal funding became available. The program is now called the Indigenous Rangers Program.
No two Indigenous ranger programs are alike—each is locally led and grounded in Traditional Owner priorities. The program of work can include burning to prevent large wildfires or maintain cultural practices and care for Country.
Rangers look after cultural sites and culturally important species, and protect threatened species by managing threats, monitoring how populations are faring and undertaking surveys and research to find out more about them.
Rangers and researchers have worked together to combine Indigenous knowledge with new technologies such as drones, satellite imagery and environmental DNA to better understand how Country is changing and inform its care.
Ranger programs also create local jobs, stronger community governance and opportunities for Elders to pass on language, cultural knowledge and practical skills to younger generations. These programs show that caring for Country can deliver environmental, cultural and social benefits.
Many Indigenous Protected Areas welcome visitors, offering cultural and nature-based tourism, walking, camping, fishing and guided experiences. Access rules vary. Some have restricted access at certain times or require permission to enter. These arrangements reflect Indigenous ownership and management.
How are these areas funded?
Like many other protected areas, IPAs are publicly funded. The Australian government gives funds to declare and manage new IPAs through protected area and Indigenous ranger programs. Some state governments provide extra support to ranger teams.
However, these funds usually cover only a fraction of the costs of managing Country in this way. IPAs with ranger programs receive just over A$1 per hectare from government funding. By comparison, national park funding varies from around $16 per hectare in Queensland to $58 per hectare in NSW. State governments largely fund national parks.
Many Indigenous organizations try to augment funding with income from carbon projects, philanthropic grants, research partnerships and environmental management contracts. This financial uncertainty creates a large administrative workload.
Can we make these areas even stronger?
As this approach to conservation matures, our growing reliance on IPAs as a key conservation approach should be matched by increased funding and capability support.
It also makes sense to invest more in monitoring and reporting to track environmental, cultural and social benefits, and to pinpoint any areas to strengthen. Better data will also help policymakers know how Australia is tracking toward our commitments to the Global Biodiversity Framework.
Indigenous Protected Areas are working well. But they're not the answer to every conservation challenge. They complement but do not replace other protected areas. The complex land tenures of the more heavily cleared and densely populated areas on Australia's east coast make it more challenging to declare new IPAs here, for instance.
As Australia works toward its conservation goals, it will rely more and more on Indigenous Protected Areas. But we believe the success of these areas speaks to something much deeper—the fact that Australia's oldest systems of caring for Country are still among the most effective ways to conserve nature.
