title: Eric Terena, el DJ indígena que denuncia el silenciamiento de la Amazonía | ENTREVISTA
content:
- El DJ y productor sonoro y musical Eric Terena fue uno de los ponentes de la conferencia TEDxAmazônia, que se realizó del 27 al 30 de agosto en Baños, Ecuador.
- Pertenece al pueblo indígena terena, de Mato Grosso, Brasil, desde donde empezó una carrera en el activismo y la comunicación para defender los derechos de los pueblos indígenas.
- En entrevista con Mongabay Latam, cuenta que en ese camino entendió que la preservación de los sonidos de la Amazonía y la música indígena contribuyen a cuidar la existencia de los pueblos.
- Ahora lleva DJ sets con estos sonidos a todo el mundo, mientras construye nuevos proyectos destinados a fortalecer a los artistas indígenas.
En un escenario en el que cada ponente contó con un guión y una ficha nemotécnica, Eric Terena improvisó su charla. Era el tercer día del TEDxAmazônia y había escuchado a líderes indígenas amazónicos hablar sobre sus pueblos y las iniciativas que están llevando a cabo para defenderlos de las industrias extractivas. Sintió que el texto lleno de datos científicos que había preparado no tenía cabida.
Leer más | Día Internacional de los Primates: tres proyectos para salvarlos del tráfico y la pérdida de hábitat
Entonces habló sobre el vínculo entre el sonido y el origen del pueblo terena, al que pertenece, en Mato Grosso, Brasil. “El pueblo terena se organiza a través del canto de nuestros chamanes”, dijo ante un público de 200 personas. Vestía un traje negro y usaba una gran corona de plumas rojas que se extendía hasta su espalda.
“La música está relacionada con la cura, hoy queremos que se entienda como el canto sagrado del pueblo terena”, continuó. Sin embargo, las lenguas de los pueblos indígenas, materia prima de esos cantos, están amenazadas por la migración inducida por el cambio climático, como lo confirmaron científicos neozelandeses en un estudio publicado en 2024.
Además, las máquinas que deforestan, minan y extraen recursos de los territorios indígenas generan un impacto sonoro que Terena llama “masacre acústica”. Esta disrupción afecta a los procesos ecológicos, aseguró.
Por eso, desde hace unos seis años se dedica a registrar los sonidos, la música y los cantos de los pueblos indígenas amazónicos para preservarlos y así mantener la continuidad de las culturas, contó en conversación con Mongabay Latam, tras su charla.
Su trabajo en la defensa de los derechos de los pueblos indígenas comenzó mucho antes. A los 19 años se unió al Movimiento Indígena del Clima de Brasil y después se convirtió en miembro fundador de Mídia Indígena, un colectivo de comunicación indígena. Desde ese espacio se vinculó con el diseño de sonido para reportes, películas y campañas.
Después dio el salto como DJ, actividad que le ha servido para hacer “artivismo” y, al llevar los sonidos de la selva a todo el mundo, demostrar que los pueblos indígenas amazónicos existen y siguen defendiendo sus territorios. Ahora, con 32 años, busca crear oportunidades para más artistas indígenas.
Mongabay Latam se reunió con Terena en Baños, Ecuador, donde se realizó la quinta edición del TEDxAmazônia, la primera fuera de Brasil.
—¿Cómo sonaba el pueblo terena antes?
—El pueblo terena tenía una tradición muy importante: cantábamos y también creábamos nuestros propios medios para cultivar la comida y mantener la sociedad más involucrada colectivamente.
Esto parte de la mitología del pueblo terena, porque Yurikoyuvakái nos sacó de un hoyo y nos enseñó a usar el fuego, a organizarnos, y también nos enseñó la parte más importante, que es involucrarse como una sociedad con dos mitades, que son los xumonó, más asociados a las bromas y a la fiesta, y los sukirikionó, que se enfocan en la estrategia, en entender la tecnología para la construcción de la sociedad indígena terena y dejar un legado milenario de adaptación.
Hoy estamos enfrentando los fuegos y la demarcación de las tierras de los pueblos terena. Antes nosotros teníamos una región muy grande donde vivíamos y ahora vivimos en una reserva mantenida por el Gobierno hasta que el Estado demarque nuestros territorios. Somos 2000 habitantes indígenas en mi comunidad y vivimos en 30 000 hectáreas, no más.
Entonces esto ha cambiado toda la realidad, incluida la preservación de nuestra identidad, porque no podemos manejar nuestros instrumentos, porque no hay más árboles ni la piel para hacer el tambor que guía nuestra danza. No hay animales por cuenta del fuego y por las haciendas y monocultivos cerca de nuestros territorios.
Eso ha cambiado mucho cómo nuestra visión se está adaptando en esta realidad contemporánea que vivimos. A pesar de estos problemas, estamos ahí cultivando y manteniendo laboratorios con jóvenes, por ejemplo de cine, y también haciendo monitoreo de territorio con drones y micrófonos para medir la densidad sonora de nuestros territorios, o sea, avanzamos mucho, pero todavía tenemos mucho por luchar.
—¿Desde cuándo viven en una reserva?
—Desde 1988, cuando la Constitución de Brasil estableció que el Estado debía demarcar y devolver las tierras indígenas en cinco años. Ya pasaron más de 35 años y estamos esperando que la Justicia brasileña nos reconozca legalmente como parte de este territorio. Esta lucha es transversal e involucra muchos saberes.
—¿Eso quiere decir que ha vivido toda su vida en una reserva?
—Yo viví en la reserva hasta los 8 años y después fui a la ciudad, porque mi familia creó una asociación en la capital [Campo Grande], donde creamos la primera institución urbana indígena de Mato Grosso del Sur.
Sigo teniendo una casa en la comunidad igualmente, pero vivo como una doble vida. Voy a la ciudad por la universidad, por el trabajo y por los DJ sets. Regreso a mi comunidad donde tengo una casa especial para grabar los sonidos. Además, hay un estudio para monitoreo de la biodiversidad.
—¿Cómo graba? ¿Se interna en la selva para registrar sonidos?
—Antes grababa con una [grabadora] Zoom. Ahora para el diseño de sonido uso micrófonos y amplificadores para grabar desde los bosques directamente. También invito a artistas para una inmersión y ellos producen música tradicional y también con instrumentos, semillas. Tengo todo lo que necesito para grabar desde hace dos años.
Además, tengo un proyecto de bioacústica con el que se hace monitoreo. Tenemos cajas con micrófonos instalados que capturan no solo sonidos, sino también frecuencias. En la computadora procesamos los datos de las frecuencias y recreamos la densidad sonora del ambiente. Podemos saber si hay fuego o deforestación.
El único problema es que no tenemos muchos fondos para implementarlo en más territorios. Logramos tener esto en nuestra comunidad, pero también en algunas partes de Ecuador para un test.
El próximo paso es conectar la herramienta a internet inalámbrico. Por el momento el único camino es usando el wifi de Elon Musk y no queremos estar con Starlink en estos territorios porque los datos son muy sensibles, principalmente si nosotros estamos identificando frecuencias de mineros, deforestación, motosierras.
—¿Ya descubrieron deforestación, minería?
—En nuestra comunidad no hay minería, pero hay minería amparada por el Gobierno en Corumbá, una ciudad muy cercana. En nuestras comunidades hay deforestación, incendios y también mucho ganado, o sea, eso es complicado porque hace un cambio a un escenario climático devastador.
Las áreas que no están dentro de nuestros territorios están como desiertos, no hay sonidos. Esto empieza a amenazar nuestros territorios porque la invasión avanza ilegalmente. En otros territorios, que antes eran haciendas y que nosotros retomamos, sembramos árboles e hicimos agroforestería. El escenario estaba cambiando, pero para medir el sonido hay que tener puntos referenciales y recién empezamos. Calculamos que en los próximos 10 años sabremos qué cambió.
—¿Cómo se ven esas frecuencias de la deforestación, de la ganadería?
—Tenemos un plugin para medir las frecuencias y podemos ver que la frecuencia está cambiando. En momentos está roja por cuenta del sonido alto y en otras ocasiones está verde porque el sonido es directo.
Lo más complicado es que al estar en una comunidad muy cerca de la parte urbana, a veces tenemos ruidos externos. O sea, esos sonidos externos también están incomodando y cambiando la biodiversidad. Como dije en la presentación, a veces no hay comunicación entre los animales, no hay reproducción y esto daña todo un ecosistema porque estos animales se van a alejar, van hacia un área muy aislada de nuestra comunidad. Este impacto es más inmediato, podemos mirarlo sin este equipamiento.
—¿Qué significa el silencio para el pueblo terena?
—El silencio responde a un mecanismo de silenciamiento. Hay un mecanismo de silenciamiento para destruirnos o perjudicarnos. Para nosotros no hay silencio, hay otro ruido más bajo, hay ruido de la naturaleza. Muchos dicen que van al bosque para estar relajados y escuchar el silencio de la naturaleza, pero la música de la naturaleza es muy alta.
En los pueblos indígenas, a medida que crece la ciudad, que avanza la ganadería, los incendios, hay más silencio. Hay un sonido de desierto, con más vientos, más insectos que están cerca de los monocultivos y que están ocupando el sonido de la naturaleza.
—¿Cómo reacciona su comunidad a su música?
—Les gusta porque la parte más contemporánea ya está en nuestro territorio hace años. Ya hay un forró terena. El forró es un estilo de música para bailar en pareja. También hay otros estilos como el sertanejo de Brasil o el reguetón de América Latina, pero con artistas indígenas. Además, hay otros ritmos dominados por indígenas, quienes están grabando en sus propios idiomas.
O sea, no inventé nada nuevo, pero estoy muy popular porque estaba involucrado en festivales de música electrónica, o sea, estaba haciendo world music y conectando con diseño de sonido, con muchas películas.
La comunidad se siente representada. Mi familia tradicional viene de un grupo de chamanes musicales y mis primos también tienen bandas, grupos de rock, pero no son tradicionales. Yo solo sigo este camino porque tengo una conexión más sagrada con la tradición. También son muy felices porque cuando estoy en Brasil hay fiesta.
—En su música hay sonidos del bosque, hay voces, cantos, ¿qué otros sonidos están?
—Como tenemos micrófonos sensibles, también grabamos, por ejemplo, palos, porque la humedad de cada región puede producir palos que al chocar hacen sonidos diferentes y crean frecuencias especiales.
Con Sarayaku estuve inmerso y aislado grabando un par de días en los bosques con Taki Supay, un rapero indígena, para que no produzcamos solamente rap, sino que el BPM [Pulsos Por Minuto] sea el mismo de la sensación de estar dentro de la comunidad. Sarayaku está como a 90 BPM.
—¿Midió la frecuencia?
—Sí, en el compás, cuando escuchas los pájaros, están en calma, pero con los kuikuro, con los karapó [pueblos indígenas de Brasil] pasó a ser más rápido, como 120 o 130 BPM.
Entonces no estoy dedicado directamente a un estilo. No hago tecno, no hago electro, no hago electronic dance music, yo soy indígena y busco crear música en el ritmo de la comunidad, en el tempo de la comunidad, ya sea que esté en la Amazonía o como ahora que estoy produciendo con músicos de Otavalo [de los Andes de Ecuador], que tienen un ritmo más parecido a la cumbia. Entonces hago arreglos y busco instrumentos que se traduzcan directamente a la identidad del pueblo con el que estamos creando la música.
—¿Cuál es el BPM del pueblo terena?
—Ahora es como 62. Antes coexistía en mayor medida la música de baile en pareja tradicional y la música de los chamanes, que tiene 30, 60 BPM y a veces no tiene constancia, es muy aleatorio.
—¿Cómo reacciona el público a su música?
—¡Dios mío! Las personas me abordan después del concierto y me dicen que nunca escucharon los sonidos de la Amazonía. Se emocionan mucho, es muy impactante porque hay mucha gente que no conoce de la Amazonía, que no sabe de su existencia. Fui a 26 países de Europa y de África, y solo cuando me ven con las plumas se dan cuenta de que la Amazonía y los pueblos indígenas todavía existen. Ahora saben que estamos fortalecidos por la música.
—¿Qué proyectos está preparando?
—En este camino con comunicadores indígenas y otros grupos estuve visitando comunidades de América Latina y escuchando que ha pasado lo mismo, porque ellos estaban perdiendo sus idiomas y necesitaban comunicación para resguardarlos.
Filmamos, grabamos y tenía esta sensibilidad para la música. O sea, después de completar las campañas para ayudar y fortalecer la identidad musical local, empecé a crear estos bancos de sonidos de cada comunidad para, en el futuro, intentar hacer colaboraciones que amplifiquen la lucha con el apoyo de colaboradores externos.
Fue un desafío hasta hace un mes, cuando se concretó un proyecto. Teníamos la idea de crear una plataforma musical y de sonido pública para que el mundo pueda acceder legalmente a los archivos y no sean robados por plataformas de la industria musical que explotan la cultura. Este es un mecanismo para que tengamos herramientas para encontrar sonidos directamente y conectar con las comunidades.
—¿Esta herramienta ya está al aire?
—No, estamos produciéndola junto con Lanceros Digitales. Ellos están programando el diseño de la plataforma, va a ser open source. Son indígenas y creemos que así no vamos a ser distorsionados por la industria.
El proyecto inicial es identificar artistas, chamanes y personas que han hecho música sanadora para cuidar y curar personas. Estamos catalogando sonidos. Vamos a avanzar también a tener una plataforma de artistas, pero no como las plataformas conocidas, que son agresivas, pagan poco y sacan mucha plata. No queremos eso, queremos que todos los derechos sean de las comunidades.
Vamos a tener artistas de toda América, desde Canadá hasta la punta de América del Sur, pero también sabemos que hay artistas en África, estamos hablando con samis del norte de Europa y con gente de Asia también. Intentamos tenerlo para febrero de 2027.
Vamos a coordinar con las comunidades para que ellos no sean dañados en ningún momento. Y quizás si hay algún riesgo, vamos a parar y reconstruir, porque queremos avanzar con las comunidades de América Latina para mantener este legado.
—¿Qué le gustaría hacer en el futuro?
—Tengo otros proyectos, pero este de amplificar y crear oportunidad para otros [músicos] indígenas creo que va a ser un gran proyecto de mi vida para crear un legado en un camino donde las personas van a querer seguir después y también replicar esto en sus comunidades, porque nosotros somos creadores, pero no impedimos que otros también creen.
Los sueños van a seguir. Para mi pueblo el sueño es muy importante para guiar nuestro camino. Yo no soñé hasta ahora qué va a pasar en el futuro, hasta que no tenga un sueño, seguiré en este proyecto.
*Imagen principal: Eric Terena es activista del pueblo terena y DJ. Trabaja con sonidos amazónicos. «La idea es que hagamos canciones, que nos encontremos haciendo revolución musical», afirmó. Foto: cortesía Eric Terena

title: One Door to the State: Ethiopia’s Leap Toward Seamless, Citizen-Centered Public Service
content:
One Door to the State: Ethiopia’s Leap Toward Seamless, Citizen-Centered Public Service
Addis Ababa, September 22, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia is reshaping the way citizens access government services through MESOB, a digital public-service platform designed to bring multiple services together under a single, more accessible system and place citizens at the center of public-service delivery.
MESOB represents a shift from navigating separate institutions and fragmented service channels toward a more unified digital gateway through which citizens can access government services.
The platform is part of Ethiopia’s broader digital transformation, which seeks to use technology not simply to digitize existing procedures, but to make public institutions more accessible, responsive and efficient.
Launched by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed last year, MESOB has expanded across the regional states, extending its reach beyond Addis Ababa and creating a national framework for integrated digital service delivery.
At its core, MESOB addresses one of the longstanding challenges of public administration: the need for citizens to move from office to office, institution to institution and process to process to obtain services that are often interconnected.
By bringing services into a common digital environment, the platform seeks to reduce that fragmentation and simplify the citizen’s journey through government.
The initiative also reflects a broader change in Ethiopia’s understanding of digital government. As the country builds its digital infrastructure, expands digital identity through Fayda and accelerates the adoption of digital payments and other technology-enabled services, the emphasis is increasingly shifting from individual digital systems toward an interconnected public-service ecosystem.
MESOB’s significance therefore extends beyond the technology underpinning the platform. It is part of an effort to redesign the interface between citizens and public institutions, making government services more accessible while strengthening the ability of institutions to deliver them through modern, coordinated systems.
The platform was among Ethiopia’s digital innovations showcased internationally in 2026, including at HUAWEI Connect in Shanghai, where MESOB demonstrated the country’s efforts to develop integrated digital public services as part of its wider technological transformation.
This emerging architecture is being built alongside a rapidly expanding digital economy. Ethiopia has recorded major growth in digital transactions and telecommunications access, while national initiatives such as the 5 Million Coders program are expanding the pool of citizens equipped to participate in the digital economy.
The convergence of digital identity, connectivity, payments, skills and integrated government services is creating the foundations for a public sector increasingly capable of operating through digital channels.
For citizens, the promise of MESOB lies in making government less fragmented and more accessible. For institutions, it offers a framework for coordinating services and reducing duplication. For the country’s wider digital transformation, it represents another step toward a state in which technology becomes an everyday instrument for connecting citizens with public institutions.
Ethiopia’s digital transformation is thus moving beyond the question of whether government services can be placed online. The larger question is how government itself can be reorganized around the needs of citizens in an increasingly digital society.
MESOB is emerging as one expression of that shift: one door to the state, designed to make the state easier to reach.

title: Public money needs new job in Africa agriculture
content:
Africa's agricultural sector accounts for roughly a fifth of the continent's GDP yet receives less than 5.0 per cent of commercial bank lending. For two decades, guarantee funds, blended finance facilities, and donor-backed risk-sharing mechanisms have worked to close that gap, with real but uneven progress. Now the risk landscape they were built for is shifting, and the tools need to shift too.
Three lessons stand out from years of engagement with banks and value chain financing. Guarantees alone don't move money; capacity does: a $6.9 million guarantee facility in Kenya unlocked a $32 million loan portfolio only because it was paired with technical assistance for banks and borrowers.
Partner selection matters as much as guarantee size: risk-sharing with well-capacitated banks achieved roughly 10 times leverage, more than double the Kenya ratio. And some of the most valuable work isn't the money at all: absorbing the risk of untested approaches early, then sharing what worked, is a public good in itself.
This experience was mostly built handling idiosyncratic risk, meaning one farmer's bad season or one client's default, which banks can increasingly manage with better data.
But a different risk is growing faster: systemic, covariate risk (variable not of primary interest) that hits an entire region at once, as seen this year in fertiliser price shocks from the Iran conflict's disruption of trade routes, and a super El Niño building for late 2026 into 2027.
No bank can diversify away a risk that hits its whole loan book at once. That isn't a confidence problem private capital will eventually solve; it's structural, and public capital is specifically suited to absorb it.
African governments have already committed to this. The Kampala CAADP Declaration calls for at least 10 percent of public expenditure to go toward agrifood systems, with $100 billion mobilised by 2035, and names resilience to climate, health, and economic shocks as a core pillar.
The complication: this is the third time the target has been set, after Maputo in 2003 and Malabo in 2014, and tracking already shows some regions falling short again. What needs to change is what the money is spent on.
Much of today's agricultural support, in Africa and among OECD countries alike, isn't idle; it's actively working against resilience.
Globally, governments spend more than $840 billion a year supporting agriculture, and roughly two-thirds of producer-level support comes in the most market-distorting forms: payments tied to specific commodities or inputs rather than outcomes.
Coupled support like this discourages the diversification that builds climate resilience and locks farmers into patterns that make sense only as long as the subsidy lasts.
In Africa, input subsidy programs remain politically popular and fiscally significant, but they're structured around maintaining current yields rather than building the buffers, such as soil health, water management, and diversified income, that let farmers absorb a bad season without a full-blown crisis.
This is why the case isn't simply "find money to redirect toward guarantees." It's "recognize that some of what we're already spending is making the problem worse."
The lessons from guarantee work don't need to be discarded; they need redirecting. Three shifts would move guarantee mechanisms from covering generic default risk to managing climate risk specifically.
Trigger design tied to climate events, not just loan performance. Guarantees can use parametric or index-based triggers, such as rainfall thresholds, satellite-observed drought indices, and temperature anomalies, that release coverage automatically when a covariate climate event hits a region, rather than waiting for it to show up loan by loan.
Regional parametric insurance schemes have already shown payouts reaching governments within weeks of a confirmed drought or cyclone.
Layered capital stacks that separate ordinary risk from tail risk.
A guarantee facility can carry a first-loss tranche for ordinary credit risk, and a second, climate-specific tranche, potentially reinsured regionally or globally, that activates only for systemic, weather-driven losses. Donors absorbing the first-loss layer can catalyse several times that amount in commercial lending banks would otherwise consider too risky, so scarce public capital concentrates on the risk private markets can't diversify away.
Conditioning guarantee eligibility on resilience-building practices. Coverage, or preferential pricing on it, can be tied to farmers adopting practices that measurably reduce climate exposure: drought-tolerant varieties, soil and water conservation, diversified cropping. This turns the guarantee from a purely financial tool into one that actively drives the resilience it's meant to protect.
Each of these mechanisms depends on observing, at scale and low cost, what farmers are actually doing, something that used to require expensive field verification.
AI tools combining satellite imagery, weather models, and yield analysis can now verify farming conditions for millions of smallholders far more cheaply and extend to guarantee design: confirming whether a farmer planted a drought-resilient variety, setting more accurate localized triggers, and scoring producers without formal credit histories.
None of this requires new money nobody can find. It requires applying what guarantee work has already taught us, about leverage, partner selection, and paired capacity-building, to the risk that's actually growing, using tools only now becoming affordable. Ordinary risk is a job for banks and better data. Climate shocks are a job for public capital, structured to unlock private capital. The Kampala Declaration already gives us the vehicle. The question is whether we finally use it.
Martien Van Nieuwkoop is a member of the AGRA Board of Directors

title: The Amandelboom Basters’ forgotten Northern Frontier story: A 19th-century tragedy
content:
During one of my first visits to the small Karoo town of Williston, Elsa van Schalkwyk, the local town historian, alerted me to a forgotten history of the Northern Cape frontier involving the “Basters” of mixed Khoi and European ancestry who lived at the German Rhenish mission in Amandelboom (renamed Williston in 1883) for much of the 19th century. The Amandelboom Basters were a prosperous and independent livestock-owning community who were pushed off their land in the late 1860s and decided to trek more than 1,000km northwards to Rehoboth in what is now Namibia.
While doing research for my book Letters of Stone I made the startling discovery that in 1908, the year the Nama and Herero genocide ended, the Rehoboth Baster community had been measured and photographed by the German physical anthropologist Eugen Fischer, who later became Hitler’s most senior racial scientist. Fischer’s career as a leading international eugenics scientist soared after he published his ethnography on the Rehoboth Basters in 1913. From 1928 to 1942, Fischer was the director of Berlin’s notorious Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Anthropology, Human Heredity and Eugenics. During World War 2 the Institute had received eye specimens and blood samples from Auschwitz from one of its postdoctoral researchers, Dr Josef Mengele. These strange and disturbing historical entanglements had made me even more curious about the little-known history of this forgotten frontier town.
Reclaiming the past
There are, of course, many forgotten histories in South Africa. There are also many attempts to reclaim buried pasts through grassroots heritage initiatives. One such initiative is taking place on Heritage Day in Williston and includes activities such as indigenous games, potjiekos, dermbraai and a roosterbrood competition. Those who attend will also be able to see 19th-century rock engravings on a nearby farm where the Amandelboom pastoralists once lived. Not much is known in the town about these rock engravings or the herders who inscribed the landscape with these impressive images.
ROCS, a local NGO based in Williston’s Coloured township of Amandelboom, is using this year’s Heritage Day to engage with this forgotten history. As Reggie Nutt, the founder of ROCS, told me: “Knowing where your people come from is vital in a community like Amandelboom, which has massive unemployment, poverty, substance abuse and a sense of hopelessness and despair amongst many youth.” But the history of Amandelboom does not easily lend itself to a straightforward heritage narrative of victims and villains. Instead, it is a complicated story that raises all sorts of troubling questions and ethical challenges.
In the early decades of the 19th century, increasing pressure of overgrazing and drought in the Cape Colony resulted in Baster and Boer pastoralists moving into this area beyond the colonial border. By the 1860s the Basters’ access to their communal pastures was increasingly threatened by trekboers and colonial land policies that ultimately resulted in their displacement. Crown Land laws of this period required Amandelboom Basters to pay for land surveying and registration, which they could not afford. Rather than be turned into landless farmworkers, they trekked to Rehoboth where they established their own Christian settlement.
You will not find anything about this Great Trek from Amandelboom to Rehoboth in school history books, museums or tourist brochures. For that history you will need to consult Dr Herbst’s (2004) Stellenbosch University PhD thesis. Herbst begins his account in 1845 with the establishment of the Rhenish mission in Amandelboom (now Williston) and ends in 1868 with the abandonment of the mission, and the trek of its Baster congregants to German South West Africa. Herbst, who grew up in Williston, wrote his thesis in Afrikaans and never published it. As a result, his dissertation has had minimal public exposure. Although historians Nigel Penn (1995) and Martin Legassick (2010) have written extensively about the Northern Frontier as a culturally diverse, contested and interstitial space where friends and foes were not always defined by “race”, the history of Amandelboom is far less written about or known.
Another source for this forgotten history is the landscape itself. You can find material traces of this buried past inscribed in the stone-domed corbelled houses and 19th-century rock engravings at Grootfontein farm some 40km northeast of Williston. Grootfontein, the original site of the Rhenish Mission Station, has been studied by University of Cape Town archaeologists Vuyiswa Lupuwana and Simon Hall (2019). They interpret these stone corbelled houses and rock engravings as evidence that Baster pastoralists inhabited both Victorian Christian and Khoi identities. The engravings include depictions of ox wagons, Victorian dress, European-style domestic architecture and images of Khoi initiation rituals and rainbulls. What these images of Victorian dress and corbelled houses suggest is that these nomadic pastoralists aspired to a modern Christian lifestyle of dignity, respectability and acceptance as subjects of the British Crown. But this was not to be because of the rigid racial hierarchies and discrimination of colonial rule.
Understanding a tragedy
The story of the two-decade-long Amandelboom mission can be understood as a tragedy of ambiguous belonging that culminated in Baster exclusion and displacement. From this perspective, the tragedy was that Basters had voluntarily assimilated into a modern Christian identity with the belief that this would help them secure protection from the British Crown. Taking on this identity involved wearing modern dress, bible reading, paying tax, carrying firearms and participating in Boer Commando massacres against the San. In their strivings to secure a better position within the racial hierarchy of the white colonial order, the Basters participated in acts of colonial collaboration and Commando violence that failed them in the end. Ultimately, they came no closer to being accepted within the white colonial social order. A similar situation unfolded in German South West Africa in the early 1900s when the Rehoboth Basters sided with the genocidal German forces against the Nama and Herero.
The other aspect of this tragedy concerns the institutional blind spots and shortcomings of the Rhenish missionaries that the Amandelboom Basters enlisted. Based on four months of intensive research in the Rhenish Mission Society Archives in Barmen, Germany, Herbst concluded that the Basters did not invite the missionaries to Amandelboom in 1845 solely for their spiritual teachings. Instead, the invitation was part of a pragmatic strategy aimed at navigating a violent and hostile colonial frontier where Afrikaner trekboers with the large herds were increasingly intruding onto the Basters’ vital water fountains and communal pastures. It was hoped that the missionaries would be effective mediators, brokers and advocates on their behalf and help them acquire protection from the British Crown. As it turned out, the Rhenish missionaries were ill-equipped for this task.
Herbst writes that by privileging spiritual concerns, the missionaries totally underestimated the impact of local ecological and political circumstances on the mission. Instead, the missionaries were bent on turning the Amandelboom pastoralists into a sedentary Christian community of cultivators and artisans along the lines of the Rhenish model of Christian settlement in the Wupper Valley of Germany. This determination was reinforced by the successful establishment in the 1830s of small-scale agricultural and shoe and tannery industries at the Rhenish mission at Wuppertal in the Western Cape. However, the Amandelboom missionaries failed to grasp the influence of the agroecological conditions of the Karoo drylands. Their German model of sedentary settlements of cultivators and small-scale industry was unworkable in the drought-prone Karoo. By contrast, the indigenous practice of nomadic pastoralism that they denigrated as “aimless wandering” was ecologically appropriate for this arid region.
The missionaries’ fixation on spiritual matters also meant that they did not have the political and strategic savviness to negotiate the escalating conflicts between white trekboer and Baster pastoralists over water points and communal pastures. They were also unable to address another sharp line of division that had begun to surface. Since the early decades of the 19th century, a class of merino wool farmers from the Beaufort West district were increasingly competing with pastoralists over access to water and land. These commercial wool farmers, and those within the colonial state who represented the interests of a growing wool export industry, lobbied for the introduction of private property laws and the enclosure of the communal rangelands. The culmination of this pressure was the passing of the 1865 Crown Lands Act. Later, the Fencing Act of 1883, and the introduction of technologies of fencing, windmills and boreholes ensured that modern livestock and wool farming would replace nomadic pastoralism (Archer 2000; Beinart 2003; Van Siddert 2002).
In the mid-1860s, the missionaries had stood by helplessly as the Basters lost access to their water points and grazing lands due to competition with other pastoralists as well as colonial land laws. It was this that led the Basters to decide to defend their autonomy by trekking to Rehoboth where, in 1872, they established a modern Christian ethno-state with a representative Baster council and constitution.
Herbst concludes in his doctoral thesis that the Basters were both devout Christians and astute pragmatists. They had invited the Rhenish missionaries because they believed they could help them negotiate inclusion and belonging as subjects of the British Crown. In many respects, the relationship between the Basters and the Rhenish missionaries mirrors the historical experiences of the Griquas, the Basotho under Moshoeshoe and the Batswana under Khama III. In each of these cases, missionaries were enlisted by indigenous communities as part of what the historian Paul Landau (2010) analyses as a pragmatic politics of belonging, inclusion and protection. Landau notes that precolonial and 19th-century southern African politics was not defined by fixed ethnic or tribal affiliations, but instead was shaped and mediated by shifting traditions of strategic and pragmatic mobilisation, alliance and amalgamation.
The tragedy of this story is that even though these nomadic pastoralists aspired to modern Christian respectability and acceptance as subjects of the British Crown, and even though they collaborated with Boer Commandos in San massacres, they were abandoned by both the missionaries and colonial authorities who failed to protect them. This 19th-century Northern Frontier history, which blurs the lines between victims and perpetrators, is important to engage with precisely because of the challenges it poses for reclaiming cultural heritage. DM

title: Verhalen van Jip en Janneke komen in het Urks uit
content: De verhalen van Jip en Janneke worden in het Urks uitgebracht. Begin oktober verschijnt het boek met de titel Vor alteed maos (Voor altijd vrienden). Eerder verschenen de verhalen van Annie M.G. Schmidt al in het Twents en het Sallands. De Urker uitgave is daarmee de derde Nedersaksische editie. Met deze vertalingen willen de betrokken organisaties regionale talen onder jongeren levend houden. Mensen uit Urk Klaas Barends schreef één Jip en Janneke-verhaaltje in het Urks voor een bundel met Nedersaksische vertalingen. Het smaakte naar meer en al snel kwam hij op het idee voor een volledig Jip en Janneke-boek in het Urks. Barends zocht mensen om hem te helpen bij het vertalen. Het moesten mensen uit Urk worden die de doelgroep, kinderen uit Urk, goed begrijpen. Hij kreeg acht reacties op een oproep in de krant. "Het leuke aan de aanmeldingen was dat veel mensen in het onderwijs werkten", vertelt Barends aan Omroep Flevoland. Niet ieder woord De groep van negen Urkers boog zich over de vertalingen. Niet ieder woord kon direct vertaald worden. Als voorbeeld geeft Barends de heg waardoor Jip en Janneke in het begin van het boek kruipen. "Daar is niet een letterlijke Urker vertaling voor. Dan gingen we met elkaar in discussie over welk woord we daarvoor wel moesten gebruiken." Stichting Urker Taol heeft daarna alle verhalen nagekeken en zorgde ervoor dat er qua spelling één lijn in zat. De verhalen van Jip en Janneke stammen uit de jaren 50. Tegenwoordig zijn er opvoeders die kritisch zijn op de in hun ogen ouderwetse rolpatronen in de verhalen. Zo bekommert de moeder zich vaak om het huishouden en gaat de vader naar het werk. Aan de andere kant zijn er ook opvoeders die menen dat de Jip en Janneke-verhalen tijdloos zijn. De twee sluiten vriendschap, beleven avonturen en spelen zoals dat ook nu nog gebeurt. Niet alleen onder de mensen die met Jip en Janneke zijn opgegroeid is het boek populair. Ook mensen buiten Nederland bleken interesse te hebben. Voor hen verscheen er in 2008 een Engelse vertaling van het boek.

title: Inside the ancestral home of MCA founder Tan Cheng Lock
content:
But tucked amidst the bustle of the city is a place whose significance many may not know. It is the ancestral home of Tan Cheng Lock, the statesman and nation builder who founded MCA and became a leading voice for Malaya’s Chinese community.
A firm believer in a united, multiracial Malaya, Cheng Lock championed equal citizenship and cooperation among the country’s different communities, helping lay the foundations for the nation that would emerge.
Located on 111 Jalan Tan Cheng Lock, formerly Heeren Street, the house remains in the care of his descendants, who continue to preserve it as an important part of the family’s heritage.
According to Cheng Lock’s granddaughter, Tan Siok Choo, the house dates back to 1799 and was purchased by her great-great-grandfather, Tan Choon Bock, for use as the family home in 1875.
Cheng Lock lived there, while Siok Choo grew up in nearby Klebang Besar and visited about once a week. She did not enjoy these visits much as a child, as getting there meant a 45-minute journey along winding roads crowded with bullock carts.
“We also never really got to see my grandparents very much. I only gained more appreciation for the house later in life, when I was writing a book on it,” Siok Choo, 73, told FMT Lifestyle.
From the outside, the home resembles a traditional Melaka shophouse. Above its main gate hang two paper lanterns emblazoned with the Tan family name, which Siok Choo noted also carry a message about the importance of education.
“The lanterns say, ‘If you don’t educate your son, you have a donkey. If you don’t educate your daughter, you have a pig’,” she said.
“I was very impressed by how enlightened the person who created these lanterns was, especially in placing such importance on educating women, which was certainly not the norm at the time.”
The message appears very much in keeping with the late Cheng Lock’s progressive views on women’s equality.
One of the most striking things about the house is its sheer length, stretching across three courtyards. At the heart of the central courtyard stands a towering tree which, according to Siok Choo, was planted during her grandfather’s time and continues to flourish today.
According to Siok Choo, the house also played a part in the country’s political history, with Tunku Abdul Rahman holding meetings there with Chinese educationists to discuss the future direction of education in Malaya.
Her favourite part of the house is the first hall. Taking pride of place is an ornate altar dedicated to Guan Yu, beneath a sign bearing the Chinese characters for “Spirit of Righteousness”. Also displayed there are several statues of Guan Yu, as well as Kuan Yin, the goddess of mercy.
“In the altar, we have enshrined the family values of righteousness, loyalty and integrity, mercy and compassion,” Siok Choo said.
Its walls are also adorned with reproductions of essays written by the noted Song Dynasty poet Su Dongpo, known for building the famous “Pavilion of Timely Rain” in China.
The house’s second hall, known as the Hall of Filial Remembrance, contains another altar where Siok Choo conducts Confucian ancestor-remembrance rituals. She also offers fruit and Peranakan food at the altar.
“A lot of Chinese don’t have ancestral homes any more, so I think the ancestral remembrance ceremonies are slowly dying out. That’s quite a pity,” she said.
The rooms of the house are filled with photographs, documents and personal mementoes chronicling generations of the Tan family.
Hanging in the study where Cheng Lock once wrote his speeches, for example, is a rare photograph of Sultan Ibrahim Al-Masyhur of Johor with his last wife and daughter. The photograph is inscribed with Cheng Lock’s name and was personally sent to him.
The house’s upper floor contains the bridal chamber, as well as a bedroom where former prime minister Tunku Abdul Rahman would stay whenever he visited Cheng Lock.
Siok Choo also pointed out a four-poster bed which, according to Tunku Abdul Rahman’s memoirs, was rather uncomfortable to sleep in.
Tunku, however, was apparently too kind-hearted to ever tell her grandfather about it.
Maintaining the family home over the years has been a challenging and resource-intensive task. Siok Choo recalled that during the pandemic, the house went largely unattended for three years, resulting in the deterioration of many items within.
Despite these challenges, she remains deeply attached to her family’s ancestral home and hopes it will be preserved for future generations.
“It’s more than just a house; it really shaped my grandfather and the rest of my relatives by instilling in them values that influenced their views on life and family.
“I think that’s important, and I hope it will one day be passed down to my nephews and niece.”

title: Cross-border project explores growing up after GFA
content:
A cross-border project examining what peace means to the generation that grew up after the Good Friday Agreement in 1998 will culminate in a theatrical performance that will be streamed live tomorrow, the UN's International Day of Peace.
Thirty young people aged 18-25 from North and South, who lived together during the summer, will perform 'Project Lighthouse,’ in the Hawk’s Well Theatre in Sligo.
The Hawk’s Well Director Kieran Griffiths said the project examines "what conflict means to a generation that inherited peace," while "exploring difference and hoping to celebrate it".
The production is a partnership between the Hawk’s Well Theatre, the Millennium Forum in Derry and the John and Pat Hume Foundation, supported by the Special EU Programmes Body.
The project participants, some of whom had no theatrical experience, were selected after they responded to advertisements, in a production guided by artists Abby Oliveira and Bob Kelly.
Mr Kelly describes the production as "a tasting board" of the young people’s discussions, using an open-mic format that expands into dance, movement and abstract theatre.
"What we’re hoping the audience will experience isn't so much a cohesive dramatic arc, but that they have had an encounter with these very interesting young people," he said.'
Grace Doherty from Derry City said the production "was great craic from day one," adding that it was a real success in terms of collaboration.
"Personally, for me, peace means that everyone, regardless of creed, race, religion, whatever, can just live and exist in the world without fear," she said.
Ms Doherty said participants, such as herself, were "very aware of the privilege" and "the safety" that the Good Friday Agreement brought, noting it was "talked about a lot".
She alluded to what the group believes is required for society to move forward as a key point of their discussions.
"A big issue that's been discussed is the rates of violence against women in the north, as well as the male suicide epidemic that the north is grappling with…
"So, there's a balance of being aware of the privilege that we have, while also being aware of what's needed moving forward," Ms Doherty said.
Luke O’Grady from Derry city, who has a background in writing, said he had never experienced theatre and found that he enjoyed "acting and loved improvisation."
"My understanding of peace after taking part hasn't really changed for me, but that's not a bad thing. I've always been quite an open person.
"The dialogue in the group was fantastic. I thought we all got on well, very quickly. It helped that the Sligo people had to stay in Derry; we were seeing each other every day."
Participant Kaylee Finnegan from Limavady, who composed a solo piece for the production, said "peace means collaboration".
Patrick Donlan from Ballintrillick in Co Sligo said he really enjoyed this project and hopes the group can remain in contact.
"Being up there really changes your perspective. It's a recent history. It's not something long gone, and it's something that still needs to be learned about," he said.
Evan Ennis from Dromahair in Co Leitrim said the group wrote their scenes together and will be on stage together, throughout the production.
"It’s so important to have that dialog, not just talking about differences, but being able to create, and highlight how similar we are and how brilliant it is that we can all come together."
Oleksandra Pidopryhora from Ukraine, who lives in Sligo said it was an amazing opportunity, to learn more about Irish history, and to discuss Ukraine’s situation as well.
"This is so great to see how people found this peace, after the troubles and this hard history and I wish that one day our people in Ukraine will live the same way in a peaceful country."
‘Project Lighthouse’ can be viewed online on The Hawk’s Well website tomorrow morning, however, online registration is required.
The production is also the subject of a fly-on-the-wall documentary, which will be included in a digital resource for schools, and it will inform another project, currently in development.
The White Dove, which will be staged at the Hawk’s Well Theatre and the Millennium Forum in 2029, will complete a trilogy of ‘The White Handkerchief’ and ‘Hume: Beyond Belief.’
Chief Executive of the Millennium Forum David McLaughlin said the cross-border initiative is a fantastic example of what can be achieved with a shared ambition.
"It demonstrates how collaboration across the island can strengthen the arts, create meaningful opportunities for the next generation and showcase the creativity and stories of this region on an international stage," he said.

title: Africa’s mother tongues are finding new life as youth connect with roots and relatives
content:
Associated Press
A television game show in Nigeria’s commercial hub of Lagos has an unforgiving rule: Speak English and you lose. For a U.S.-born millennial in the audience and a student of her parents’ mother tongue, the high-stakes setting is a perfect classroom.
Meanwhile, a 15-year-old Canadian speaks to a teacher about 13,000 kilometers (8,000 miles) away in Zimbabwe, learning a language her parents feared she would never speak.
“Mhoroi,” Nyashadzashe Machingura says cheerfully with a pronounced Canadian accent while greeting in Zimbabwe’s vernacular Shona.
The scenes capture a new generation of interest and entrepreneurship around African languages once pushed to the margins by decades of colonialism. Often seen as secondary to English, French and Portuguese, they are enjoying a renaissance that is also creating business opportunities.
Africa is home to over 1 billion people speaking roughly a third of the world’s languages, with between 1,500 and 3,000 across 54 countries, according to UNESCO.
Experts say the revival in some of them is driven partly by second- and third-generation Africans in the diaspora finding it easier to reconnect with their roots and communicate with older relatives, thanks to social media, online learning and entertainment.
“There were times I definitely felt left out because my family around me were all speaking Shona. And I just couldn’t understand them,” Nyashadzashe said after a lesson covering traditional greetings, proverbs and ancestral clan symbols. She said she had eaten the food and worn the traditional clothing but still felt left out.
But now her conversations with her grandparents in Zimbabwe are growing longer.
“Being able to connect with them on that level makes me really proud of my heritage,” she said.
Her Zimbabwe-based tutor, Shungu Chidovi, left her banking career in January to focus full-time on ZimbOriginal, an online platform that teaches Shona through storytelling, book clubs and “buddy pairing” exchanges.
Now she teaches about two dozen learners in Zimbabwe, Canada, Australia, South Africa, Ireland and Scotland, charging $50 a month.
The business, part of a small but growing number of online initiatives teaching African languages, emerged almost by accident. Chidovi began writing a blog about Zimbabwean traditions in 2016. Readers began asking whether she taught Shona.
“I didn’t see it at the time that I was really writing about the Shona language,” Chidovi said.
Like many in Africa, she grew up with the understanding that to get ahead she had to embrace Western languages instead of her mother tongue. English remains the dominant language for education, business and government affairs in the southern African nation that officially recognizes 16 mostly Indigenous languages.
“When you talk of Africa, you talk of English, French, Portuguese,” said Believe Mubonderi, a linguistics lecturer at Zimbabwe Open University. His research notes the importance of ensuring that African languages have a place in technologies shaping how people communicate, learn and trade.
“In most cases, African languages were sidelined. They were never exposed or modernized to be used in commerce, science and technology,” he said. “When a language has a very low status, there’s a danger that that language eventually becomes endangered.”
Governments and international organizations are trying to reverse that trend.
The African Union’s 2022 decision to adopt Kiswahili, spoken in much of east Africa, as an official working language has raised its international profile. The United Nations declared 2022-2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.
And the AU continental body and UNESCO are supporting efforts to document and revitalize African languages, including using artificial intelligence to generate and translate children’s books and teacher guides.
But there’s a steep digital disadvantage. UNESCO says only 10 languages around the world dominate the “internet ecosystem,” while less than 2% of African languages have a meaningful online presence. That leaves many with too little data to train artificial intelligence systems.
Still, momentum for change is growing, with much of it from Africans abroad.
“People of African descent have come to realize that we also have our own identity which we need to embrace and be proud of. You go on Facebook, you go on TikTok, you are seeing many different efforts,” Mubonderi said. Younger diaspora Africans “are trying by all means to revive, to revitalize, to make use of these languages.”
Chindovi said she hears that desire from children and their parents.
“When people are away from home, they long for home more than when they are home,” she said.
That hunger for connection is also reshaping culture.
In Nigeria, a game show called “Masoyinbo,” meaning “Do not speak English,” has turned Yoruba, one of the country’s most widely spoken languages, into prime-time entertainment. Contestants, including diaspora Nigerians, are tested on Yoruba language and culture, with prizes reaching thousands of dollars.
Host Olalekan Fabilola, who started the show in 2024, sees its popularity as part of a wider shift.
“If ‘Masoyinbo’ had started like 10 years ago, it wouldn’t have been what it is now,” he said. “But we are in the age of cultural resurgence. People want to go back to their roots. Everyone wants to know why, where they are from, and so it’s timely.”
Tomi Adeshokan, a New Jersey resident who is learning to perfect her Yoruba with Fabilola as a tutor, was part of the audience during a recent recording of the show. She said she lost daily exposure to Yoruba after moving out of her father’s home before the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, she joined Clubhouse just to hear the language and later began taking classes. Now she was back visiting family.
“It’s very important for us to immerse ourselves in our culture and not to fully identify with other cultures, like the American, the Western culture,” Adeshokan said.

title: The bird that changed Ecuador: how a chance discovery of a rare species helped to save many more
content:
I have to confess that I rarely enjoy birding in montane cloud forests. The birds that live in these mountainous, cool and humid habitats are masters of disguise, usually passing themselves off as a leaf or other form of foliage. But if I want to see antpittas – elusive, ground-dwelling birds that rarely show themselves – then I have no choice.
So, on a cool, cloudy morning my guide, Juan Carlos Crespo, Fredy Ramón Castillo, a local ranger, and I are standing on a steep, muddy path close to Tapichalaca Lodge, 2,500 metres above sea level in the eastern Andes, waiting for the jocotoco antpitta to emerge from the undergrowth.
Fortunately, antpittas have a soft spot for food, especially the large, juicy earthworms Castillo has placed on a low branch nearby. He calls the bird, with increasingly loud and urgent shouts of “venga, venga!” (“come on, come on!”). The minutes tick by, until I begin to wonder if this is a lost cause.
Then, out of nowhere, a plump, thrush-sized bird with a chestnut back, grey front, black crown and white face-patch materialises just a few feet away. It proceeds to gulp down the earthworms as if it has not eaten for days.
I have seen a lot of different birds, but never one that so changed the course of bird conservation. In November 1997, a group led by the influential US ornithologist Robert Ridgely was exploring this area of southern Ecuador to see what they could find.
As they ascended a forest trail at dawn, they heard the sound of a bird in the far distance. As Ridgely recalled many years later, “It had this crazy call, sounding like an owl; but we had no idea what it was, and to be honest I never thought we would find out.”
Ridgely walked ahead of the group, and heard the sound much closer than before. He recorded the call and played it back to the mystery creature, which came crashing through the dense bamboo, right out into the open.
“I knew right away that this was something really special, which no one apart from the local people had ever seen – an entirely new species to science.” It was, in fact, one of the greatest ornithological breakthroughs of the late 20th century: while new species are sometimes discovered, they are rarely so large, noisy and so obviously different from other members of their family.
Talking to local farmers, Ridgely discovered that they were familiar with the bird, which they had named “jocotoco” to represent its loud, barking call. Two years later, the species was officially described, and named the jocotoco antpitta; the scientific name, Grallaria ridgelyi, commemorating its proud discoverer.
Ridgely soon realised that if the bird was to be saved from extinction its forest home needed to be urgently protected. He and a group of like-minded friends created an organisation dedicated to saving the bird and its habitat, raising funds from donors in the US and Europe to buy and restore the land. In 1998 the Jocotoco Foundation was born.
Today, the foundation protects and manages 19 reserves throughout Ecuador, covering about 50,000 hectares (193 sq miles), and manages a further 82,000 hectares of privately and communally owned land. Together, these sites are home to more than 1,350 species of birds – that’s 80% of all those found in Ecuador, and an astonishing one in eight of all bird species on the planet, as well as many other plant and animal species. The foundation also works closely with nearby communities, employing local people as park rangers – many of whom grew up on the land they now protect – and through jobs in wildlife tourism.
The model for the foundation’s reserves is simple and very effective. First, it restores habitat by planting a variety of native trees and other plants, or in some places simply allows the vegetation to regenerate on its own. Park guards, all of whom come from local communities, protect the reserves against illegal incursions such as cattle grazing, logging and poaching, aided by new technology including camera traps and audio recorders.
They also use these to monitor the fortunes of key species, while providing nest boxes to encourage them to breed, making up for the loss of natural tree cavities while the old-growth forests are being restored.
A recent study at Canandé, in the Chocó region of north-west Ecuador, revealed that even after deforestation, nature can recover very rapidly. The study showed that in just three decades – a single human generation – of being managed for biodiversity, formerly cleared lands have recovered 90% of the biomass – the weight of all animals – and 90% of the number of species found in nearby mature forests. While the new mix of species is not fully the same as in a mature forest, 75% of the original species present in an old-growth forest have returned.
Mike Parr, the president of the American Bird Conservancy, has no doubt about the importance of this work. “Beyond safeguarding Ecuador’s rarest birds, migrating species and incredible overall biodiversity, Jocotoco’s strategic integration of ecotourism, public awareness, community engagement and scientific research are world class. They have done an amazing job covering the previously unprotected endangered species of Ecuador.”
During recent visits to Ecuador I have visited 10 of the foundation’s reserves, including those in the Chocó region north-west of Quito and Copalinga in the Amazon foothills, along with the Los Petreles reserve on San Cristóbal Island in the Galápagos, a refuge for a critically endangered seabird, the Galápagos petrel.
On a visit to Buenaventura reserve, a restored cattle ranch in the western foothills of the Andes, we went in search of an even rarer bird: the El Oro parakeet. This charismatic parrot was only discovered as recently as 1980, and has a tiny home range, with fewer than 1,000 individuals.
Another early start took us to an open area of grassland and scattered trees where the birds are known to gather. Moments later, we heard a raucous call, and there they were: several flocks totalling about 20 of these emerald-green birds, the males with a distinctive red forehead.
But even this memorable moment was eclipsed by my visit to the Chakana nature reserve, more than 4,000 metres above sea level in the páramo grasslands of the high Andes – yet just an hour south-east of Quito. On an unexpectedly fine and sunny day, against a stunning backdrop of the snow-capped Cotopaxi volcano, we enjoyed closeup views of the Ecuadorian hillstar, a specialist high-altitude hummingbird, along with nine Andean condors soaring right around us, before they rose high into the clear blue sky.
Numbers of the Andean condor, the world’s largest flying bird by a combination of weight and wingspan, have fallen rapidly in recent years, due mainly to deliberate poisoning. But here, these mighty raptors are now returning to their ancestral home.
Dr Martin Schaefer, chief executive of Jocotoco, believes that even in these dark times there is room for optimism. “The power to restore what we have lost is in our hands.”
Ian J Davidson, Americas regional director for BirdLife International, agrees. “By creating a network of protected habitat ‘arks’, Jocotoco has given these remarkable species a genuine chance not only to endure, but to recover and expand beyond their remaining strongholds.
“Their work stands as a global conservation success story, an inspiring example of what determination, science and long-term stewardship can achieve for nature.”
At a time when President Trump has withdrawn US government funding for conservation projects around the world, the Jocotoco Foundation is a classic model of how scientists and local people can work together to save endangered birds and the precious places where they live.
This article by Stephen Moss was first published by The Guardian on 13 September 2026. Lead Image: Thirty years after a US ornithologist first sighted a jocotoco antpitta, the foundation he set up to restore biodiversity is a model for conservation globally.

title: Shakira donó casi 4 millones de dólares para construir un colegio con lugar para 1700 estudiantes
content:
Shakira donó casi 4 millones de dólares para construir un colegio con lugar para 1700 estudiantes
La cantante colombiana aportó casi cuatro millones de dólares para la obra en Cartagena, Colombia; la institución educativa integra a la comunidad local desde hace más de una década
- 3 minutos de lectura'
Shakira consolidó su labor filantrópica en Colombia mediante un proyecto educativo de gran envergadura en la ciudad de Cartagena. La artista, a través de su fundación Pies Descalzos, acercó casi cuatro millones de dólares para la construcción de la Institución Educativa Lomas del Peyé. Esta obra, inaugurada en febrero de 2014, significó una inversión global de ocho millones de dólares. Según los datos oficiales, la intérprete aportó el 46% del presupuesto total, mientras que el resto del capital provino de diversos aliados estratégicos del sector público y también del ámbito privado.
El establecimiento educativo ocupa un terreno de 7780 metros cuadrados en el barrio La María, y el diseño del edificio contempló la capacidad de albergar a 1700 alumnos de diversas edades. La estructura posee 55 espacios funcionales diferenciados, los cuales brindan servicios de primera infancia, nivel primario y nivel secundario. El predio incorpora aulas especializadas, una biblioteca completa, un comedor, instalaciones deportivas aptas para la recreación y un centro destinado al uso de la comunidad. Este modelo edilicio trasciende la pedagogía tradicional para convertirse en un centro de desarrollo integral de las familias habitantes de la zona.
El impacto socioeconómico del proyecto resultó notable durante su etapa de ejecución, ya que de acuerdo con información de la Fundación Pies Descalzos, la construcción generó entre 350 y 400 empleos directos. El 60% de esta mano de obra correspondió a personas residentes en los barrios vecinos. Este dato subraya el compromiso de la iniciativa con el desarrollo local del área metropolitana de Cartagena. La obra funcionó como un motor para la economía regional durante el periodo de edificación.
A más de diez años de su apertura, la institución mantiene su vigencia: la entidad recibe cada año a más de mil niños y niñas. Durante el ejercicio 2024, los responsables de la fundación conmemoraron el décimo aniversario de la sede Lomas del Peyé. El organismo ratificó el objetivo de continuar el trabajo en el sector para mejorar el acceso y la calidad del aprendizaje de los menores. La gestión del colegio permanece activa y centraliza gran parte de las actividades sociales de la comunidad próxima al barrio La María.
La influencia de la figura pública permitió la concreción de este hito educativo en su tierra natal con un proyecto que continúa como un pilar fundamental para la escolarización local. La propuesta educativa se enfoca en transformar el entorno familiar a partir de un espacio de contención y formación. El complejo funciona como una pieza central en la red de apoyo social que sostiene la fundación.
Esta obra representa una parte significativa de la labor solidaria de la artista colombiana, quien mantiene su compromiso con el desarrollo de proyectos similares en diversas regiones de su país de origen. La estructura edilicia se conserva como una referencia en la zona por su magnitud y por la calidad de sus servicios prestados a la población. El proyecto demuestra el alcance de la inversión social cuando se articulan esfuerzos públicos y privados bajo una misma visión de futuro educativo para los sectores más vulnerables de Colombia.

title: How Assam’s Artisans Turn One Bamboo Plant Into Hundreds of Things We Use Every Day
content: 1 Plant, 100 Uses explores the many ways familiar Indian plants, leaves, fruits and trees have been part of everyday life — from food and farming to homes, traditions and natural remedies. Each story takes one plant and uncovers the surprising ways people have found it useful, often across generations. A bamboo plant can look rather ordinary. It may grow gently beside a home, along a field or across the hills of Assam, commonly becoming so familiar that people stop noticing it. But look a little closer, and the same plant can become a chair, a house, a basket, a musical instrument, paper, food, flooring or even a source of livelihood. India is home to 136 bamboo species, of which 125 are indigenous. According to the Government of India, the country has 13.96 million hectares under bamboo and is the second richest country in the world in terms of bamboo diversity. That versatility is perhaps best understood through people who have spent years working with it. In Jorhat, Assam, bamboo is not essentially a raw material for Prabhat Saikia. It has become the foundation of a business, a craft and a source of work for young artisans. From a bamboo pole to a piece of furniture When Saikia started a small bamboo and cane handicraft unit in 2006, he wanted to show that the plant growing abundantly around him could become more than an everyday utility. A bamboo plant can look rather ordinary. Photograph: (Organicbazar) His workshop now turns bamboo into furniture and decorative pieces, with around 20 young artisans working there. Some of them found a way to earn a living without leaving their villages for cities. He also learnt that bamboo’s strength depends on how it is treated. Working with the Rainforest Research Institute in Jorhat, he trained in bamboo treatment techniques and worked on making his products more durable. That made it possible for his bamboo to move beyond traditional handicrafts into furniture, cottages, and architectural spaces. The Government’s National Bamboo Mission lists construction, furniture, flooring, doors, windows, frames, trusses, and other building components among bamboo’s uses. The Indian Institute of Wood Science and Technology also notes that bamboo can be harvested in a two to four year cycle and has been used in board and panel forms for more than 1,000 documented applications. A home can begin with bamboo In many parts of India, particularly the Northeast, bamboo has long been part of the way homes are built. It can be used for walls, roofs, flooring, doors, windows, and structural components. Modern processing has also opened the door to laminated panels and engineered bamboo products. The Government of India’s National Bamboo Mission lists species used for construction, furniture, basketry, food containers, musical instruments, and other applications. This matters because bamboo is renewable and fast-growing. But using it responsibly still requires proper harvesting, treatment, and processing. Saikia’s experience is a useful reminder that only having bamboo is not enough. Skills and technology determine how much value can come from it. It can reach the dining table too Bamboo is not only something to build with. Certain species produce edible shoots, which are eaten in several parts of India and across Asia. The National Bamboo Mission lists edible shoots among the uses of species such as Melocanna baccifera, Dendrocalamus asper, and Dendrocalamus giganteus. The plant can also be made into food containers, kitchen products, and other household items. So, from the field to the kitchen, bamboo can have a place in everyday life. From craft to paper and fabric The usefulness of bamboo does not end when it leaves a craftsperson’s workshop. It is used as a raw material for pulp and paper. It can also be processed into fibres and used in textile products. The same plant can become a chair, a house, a basket, a musical instrument, paper, food, flooring or even a source of livelihood. Photograph: (Joynagar) The Telangana government’s bamboo mission lists pulp and paper, textiles, furniture, construction products and even energy production among bamboo’s applications. Its traditional uses are equally varied. Bamboo can become baskets, mats, lamps, storage products, and musical instruments. Different Indian species have their own uses, depending on their strength, size, and properties. In Assam, Saikia has taken some of these familiar forms and given them a place in contemporary homes. His furniture has reached markets beyond the state, while his skills have taken him to international workshops in Nepal. And then there is the land itself Perhaps one of bamboo’s most important uses is one we cannot always see. Its dense root system can help hold soil together and reduce erosion. Research and government-backed work in India has also explored bamboo for restoring degraded land. The Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser notes that a bamboo-based conservation system can reduce soil loss from 22 tonnes per hectare per year to 4.5 tonnes, while conserving 45 percent soil moisture. The same work records bamboo biomass production of 12 to 30 tonnes per hectare per year. Government material on bamboo also highlights its potential for carbon sequestration because of its rapid biomass accumulation. The humble plant also plays a role in protecting the ground on which people farm and live. One plant, many livelihoods The most meaningful use of bamboo is not an object at all. It is the work created around it. In Saikia’s Jorhat workshop, it passes through many hands before it becomes a finished chair or decorative piece. Artisans cut it, shape it, weave it, and polish it. Distributors take the finished products to new markets. Buyers take a piece of Assam into their homes. His story shows what happens when a resource that people have grown up taking for granted is given skill, treatment, design, and a market. The Government of India’s National Bamboo Mission has established hundreds of nurseries, treatment units, and product development and processing units as part of efforts to strengthen the bamboo economy. As of December 2024, the mission reported 528 product development and processing units and 104 treatment and preservation units. So perhaps the phrase “100 uses” is not really about counting every possible thing bamboo can become. It is about seeing the possibilities in something that has always been there. For someone like Saikia, that possibility began with a humble bamboo pole in Assam. Today, it can become a chair in Delhi, a building component, a basket, a meal, a sheet of paper or a livelihood that allows an artisan to remain close to home. In many parts of India, particularly the Northeast, bamboo has long been part of the way homes are built. Photograph: (www.vasoobambooarts.in) And sometimes, a plant becomes most valuable when we learn to look at it differently.
