title: ‘A single wrong step’: Women deminers reach where men cannot to protect children in Syria
content:
In a dry field in Syria’s Idlib countryside, Lama Haj Kaddour holds a detonator, steady and practised.
She and her all-female team have spent hours locating and safely approaching a buried landmine. A short distance away, the rest of the team waits, still and silent.
When the blast goes off, a column of smoke rises from where the mine had been.
Kaddour wears a protective vest over her clothes. Like her colleagues, she dresses fully in black with only her eyes visible, in line with social norms in Idlib.
Fourteen years of civil war have left Syria littered with landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW). The threat has followed families back to the villages they fled, even after the end of a conflict that killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions and devastated the economy.
Kaddour is one of 31 women now working in operational roles in Idlib’s demining effort, according to The HALO Trust, an international NGO involved in Syria’s demining work.
They clear landmines, survey contaminated ground and teach communities how to recognise the dangers left behind by the civil war.
Kaddour, a 33-year-old mother of three, left the Hama countryside for Idlib in 2019. She first worked with relief organisations before joining The HALO Trust.
In a conservative region like Idlib, being a woman can carry a particular advantage in demining work.
“A woman working in this field can enter local households and speak directly with women and children in ways her male colleagues often cannot, giving her direct access to a part of the community that is otherwise hard to reach in a conservative context,” Emma Pomfret, Global Media Manager for The HALO Trust, tells TRT World.
Women remain a minority in demining worldwide.
A 2019 survey of a dozen mine action operators published by the Journal of Conventional Weapons Destruction found that women made up only around 20 percent of mine action staff globally, with clearance roles particularly male-dominated.
According to Pomfret, however, more women are entering the field in Syria.
The fall of the Assad regime in late 2024 removed severe operational restrictions that had constrained HALO’s work, she says, allowing the organisation to expand training and clearance into areas including Daraa and the northwest and recruit from a much larger pool of people.
“When the Assad regime fell in December 2024, HALO opened recruitment and training to women, as we do on all of our programmes globally,” she says.
Supporting landmine survivors
In training hubs such as Daraa, women now make up about 20 percent of new demining trainees — eight out of a recent class of 40, according to Pomfret. As HALO expands beyond 250 staff nationwide, women are increasingly working as manual deminers, team supervisors, paramedics and community educators.
The shift is not only about new opportunities. Some of the women joining HALO were widowed during the war and are now the main breadwinners for their families, Pomfret says.
Kaddour's own path into demining began earlier. She started by supporting landmine survivors before training for fieldwork in 2022 and taking on the work of clearing unexploded ordnance herself.
“I could never live with the idea that a single wrong step by my children could set off a landmine that ends their lives, or takes one of their limbs,” Kaddour tells TRT World.
More than three million displaced people have returned to areas badly damaged by the conflict. Many find their homes still standing, but the roads leading to them contaminated.
Raed al-Hassoun, director of clearance operations at Syria’s National Mine Action Centre, tells TRT World that 49 landmine incidents were recorded across the country between the start of 2026 and the end of August, killing 24 people and injuring 61.
On August 31, an unexploded object detonated in the village of Faydat Ibn Muwaina in the Deir Ezzor countryside as children were handling it. Four children were killed and one was injured, according to SANA.
The Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR) says at least 3,799 civilians — including 1,000 children and 377 women — have been killed by landmines and cluster munition remnants across Syria since March 2011, with 329 of those deaths recorded since December 2024.
The highest tolls were recorded in Aleppo, with 814 deaths, followed by Raqqa with 676 and Deir Ezzor with 645. Hama, Daraa and Idlib were also among the worst affected.
According to SNHR, the Assad regime, Russian forces and terror groups have planted landmines across Syrian territory since 2011, often without marking or recording their locations.
Siba Abdul Karim, a 36-year-old mother of two who heads the non-technical survey department at The HALO Trust, says floods and heavy rains can expose or move buried mines and other war remnants.
“The danger isn’t necessarily fixed where the war left it,” she tells TRT World
“Floodwater, like what we saw in late August, can reshape the land and carry buried explosive objects with it, rendering old maps insufficient. Ground that seemed safe yesterday can become a fresh hazard after a flood or landslide.”
Abdul Karim and her colleagues have chosen to confront that danger directly.
The women say years of war have made them less afraid of the risks involved in their work.
“Every morning, I say goodbye to my children before leaving for the field. Every evening, when I walk back through the door, I give thanks that I made it home unharmed,” Abdul Karim tells TRT World.
She recalls once calming a child who had found an explosive device, reassuring him before explaining the danger of what he had found.
Also working in the field is Mariam al Asaad, 26, who is married and has an eight-year-old daughter.
For nearly four years, al Asaad has volunteered with the Syrian Civil Defence, also known as the White Helmets, conducting non-technical surveys and risk education and helping map contaminated areas. In 2022, she received specialised training in survey and munitions classification, becoming one of the first women to join Syria’s ERW teams.
Every morning, al Asaad kisses her daughter goodbye before leaving for the field. When she returns home, she faces the challenge of balancing a dangerous job with motherhood.
“I worry all the time about the balance between my daughter and this job,” she tells TRT World.
For al Asaad, the work is also personal. Her father owned land east of Idlib that was contaminated with landmines the family did not know were there.
In 2017, as fighting around Idlib eased, he returned to tend to the family’s olive grove, taking al Asaad’s younger brother, then nine years old, with him.
“A landmine exploded when my brother threw a stone at the ground. It tore into his left foot,” she says.
With no way of knowing how many more mines lay buried there, the family abandoned the land.
“My father spent his final years watching the trees go wild, and the little fruit that still fell just rotted on the ground,” she says. “We ended up buying olive oil every season, even though we had a grove that used to give us our own.”
Al Asaad believes the grief of losing access to the land took a heavy toll on her father’s health.
Waiting for the land back
In the village of Dadikh in the Idlib countryside, Abu Mohammad al Ali, 62, owns land that was once his family’s sole source of livelihood. The war has turned it into a place he can no longer enter.
He grew olive and fruit trees there, relying on the harvest to support his family, before mines and other war remnants contaminated the land.
“We used to come here at first light, plough, plant, and tend to the trees,” al Ali tells TRT World.
“Today I’m afraid to take a single step onto my own land. The trees we worked so hard to grow have died because we can no longer reach them to water them and care for them.”
According to al Ali, his land was the scene of clashes and aerial bombardment during the war.
Assad regime forces, backed by Russian air support, attempted to advance towards the edges of the village but were unable to take the area from local forces.
His land lay along the front line.
Months of fighting left the land heavily contaminated with mines and other remnants of war, making it inaccessible even after the fighting stopped.
“Fear is part of daily life for my family and everyone in the village,” he says.
He recalls an incident in 2025 when a mine exploded on his land while a child was nearby.
Since then, he has struggled with the thought that land that once fed his family could instead kill a child.
“Farmers in Dadikh live between leaving their land and losing their livelihood, or returning to it with the possibility that the next step could be their last,” he says.
“The hardest part is that when I look at my land, I still see it as it used to be. I see the trees, and I remember the seasons we used to wait for. But today I can't get close to it.”
“We just want the mines removed, and to know the land is safe before we send our children there or go back to farming it ourselves,” he adds.
Alongside clearance efforts, UNICEF and its partners are teaching children and families to recognise mine risks before demining teams can reach contaminated areas.
Fouad Mansour, a project manager at UNICEF, tells TRT World that the agency and its partners reached roughly 850,000 children, parents and caregivers with mine-risk education in 2025 and trained around 400 specialists.
“We use pictures, stories, games and visual material to turn a frightening fact into a behaviour a child can remember: don’t touch the strange object, move away from it, and tell an adult or the relevant authority,” he says.
Mansour says UNICEF works with 38 partners across mine clearance, victim assistance, risk education and advocacy.
It has also supported the development of a national risk-education framework integrated into the curriculum in coordination with Syria’s Ministry of Education.
A national effort to bring order
At the national level, Syria’s National Mine Action Centre is coordinating efforts by international and local organisations.
“We are currently developing the national standards that will govern the work of organisations in this field,” Raed al Hassoun says.
“We are also building a national information management system to collect the data that will underpin a roadmap for addressing landmine and ERW risk according to national priorities.”
Among the centre’s priorities is completing a national non-technical survey to determine the location, type and scale of contamination, amid what al Hassoun describes as limited capacity to address the problem's scale.
“Our own figures are still incomplete,” he says, adding that the national survey under way is intended to close that gap.
Military engineering teams from the Ministry of Defence and dedicated units from the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management also take part in clearance operations, he says.
“The reconstruction of Syria’s battered infrastructure depends first and foremost on resolving the mine issue,” al Hassoun says, pointing to the Jobar district of Damascus as an example.
At the request of the Damascus governorate, the centre established an operations room that brought together the HALO Trust, the International Committee of the Red Cross, teams from the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management, and Red Crescent non-technical survey teams.
Together, they cleared Jobar’s main and side roads, allowing reconstruction work to begin.

title: La ONCE recuerda que la inclusión no debe quedarse en las aulas: "Tiene que estar en el recreo, el comedor..."
content:
La ONCE recuerda que la inclusión no debe quedarse en las aulas: "Tiene que estar en el recreo, el comedor, las extraescolares..."
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
Más de 7.000 estudiantes con ceguera o con deficiencia visual grave inician estos días el nuevo curso escolar.
Más de 7.000 estudiantes con ceguera o con deficiencia visual grave inician estos días el nuevo curso escolar. El 99% de ellos lo hace en centros ordinarios, dentro de un modelo de educación inclusiva respaldado por equipos de atención educativa de la ONCE, que proporcionan los apoyos necesarios para seguir el currículo en igualdad de oportunidades.
Sin embargo, volver al colegio no significa únicamente regresar a las aulas. La experiencia educativa también se construye en otros espacios y momentos que forman parte de la vida diaria de los centros y que son fundamentales para el desarrollo personal y social del alumnado. “La jornada escolar incluye otros tiempos y actividades. El recreo, el comedor, horarios ampliados o actividades complementarias y extraescolares son esenciales para el aprendizaje y tienen una influencia decisiva en el desarrollo de la autonomía personal y de las competencias sociales”, explica Ana Llauradó, responsable de Atención Educativa de la ONCE.
Por ello, la ONCE recuerda que el alumnado con discapacidad visual tiene tanto el derecho como la necesidad de participar plenamente en todas estas actividades en igualdad de condiciones que el resto de sus compañeros.
Recreos para todos
El recreo constituye un espacio clave de convivencia y socialización. Para que sea realmente inclusivo, debe ofrecer oportunidades de juego y participación para todo el alumnado. La ONCE impulsa patios accesibles, organizados en diferentes zonas, con propuestas variadas que favorezcan la interacción y el juego compartido. Asimismo, resulta fundamental disponer de un repertorio de juegos inclusivos que puedan elegir y disfrutarse de forma autónoma, siempre con la adecuada supervisión adulta.
El comedor como espacio de autonomía
Del mismo modo, el comedor escolar representa una oportunidad privilegiada para fomentar habilidades esenciales para la vida diaria. “Espacios como el comedor permiten reforzar la autonomía del alumnado con discapacidad visual en tareas cotidianas como la alimentación o el aseo”, señala Llauradó.
Los técnicos de rehabilitación de la ONCE enseñan a estos estudiantes a desenvolverse de forma independiente según su edad y desarrollo, realizando acciones como cortar los alimentos, servirse agua o mantener hábitos de higiene personal. Además, forman a los profesionales que trabajan en estos entornos para que puedan reforzar dichas habilidades en el día a día.
Aprender también fuera del aula
Las actividades complementarias, desarrolladas dentro del horario lectivo, enriquecen el aprendizaje a través de experiencias prácticas y vivenciales. Para garantizar la participación de todo el alumnado, es importante que incorporen enfoques multisensoriales y que los materiales se preparen y adapten previamente cuando sea necesario. Las actividades extraescolares también desempeñan un papel fundamental. Son un entorno idóneo para descubrir intereses, desarrollar habilidades artísticas o deportivas y fortalecer las relaciones sociales, aspectos especialmente relevantes para el desarrollo integral del alumnado.
“Todos los espacios, tiempos y actividades que conforman la vida escolar son enormemente enriquecedores para el alumnado y, especialmente, para los estudiantes con discapacidad visual, siempre que se planifiquen teniendo en cuenta la diversidad y se incorporen estrategias y recursos que hagan efectiva la inclusión”, concluye la responsable de Atención Educativa de la ONCE.
Más de 400 profesionales al servicio de la inclusión
La ONCE cuenta con equipos específicos de atención educativa integrados por maestros y maestras, tanto de la ONCE como de las administraciones educativas, que prestan apoyo directo en los centros escolares. Su labor incluye la atención al alumnado en aspectos relacionados con la discapacidad visual o la sordoceguera, el acompañamiento a las familias y el asesoramiento al profesorado mediante herramientas, recursos y estrategias que favorecen el acceso al currículo ordinario en igualdad de oportunidades. Actualmente, más de 400 profesionales desarrollan esta tarea en todas las comunidades autónomas.
Junto al personal docente, estos equipos están formados por psicólogos, trabajadores sociales, técnicos de rehabilitación, instructores de tiflotecnología y braille, especialistas en animación sociocultural y mediadores para alumnado con sordoceguera. Todos ellos contribuyen, desde una perspectiva multidisciplinar, al desarrollo integral y la plena inclusión educativa.
Durante el curso 2025/2026 se atendió a más de 7.000 estudiantes con ceguera o con deficiencia visual, incluidos aquellos con sordoceguera o discapacidades asociadas: 1.103 en Educación infantil, 1.421 en Primaria, 1.128 en Secundaria, 298 en Bachillerato, 526 en Formación Profesional, 803 en la universidad, 1.306 en Educación Básica Obligatoria y 549 en otras enseñanzas.

title: Jews once lived lived here: When houses tell stories
content:
Jews once lived lived here: When houses tell stories
September 17, 2026Over the years, many people have passed through this fourth-floor apartment in an old Berlin building. Here, at Rosenheimer Straße 40, they have sat on the sofa and gathered around the kitchen table. They have looked out the window and let their minds wander.
Marie Rolshoven has lived here with her family since 2007. "The feeling of crossing that threshold, the same one the former residents crossed for the last time, stays with you," she says. She knows that Jews once lived here, and none of them survived the Nazi era.
Driven from their homes
After the National Socialists seized power in January 1933, it quickly became clear that Jews were considered second-class citizens under Nazi rule. Even the right to remain in their homes could no longer be taken for granted.
"A racially conscious fellow citizen cannot be expected to share a household with a Jew," the Nazi party newspaper Völkischer Beobachter wrote on September 18, 1938, claiming that landlords were therefore entitled to terminate leases without notice. On April 30, 1939, the law took effect. Jewish tenants and property owners were forced to leave their homes and move into buildings designated by the authorities, referred to in Nazi jargon as "Judenhäuser"(Jewish houses).
Several people were forcibly housed in Henny and Carl Möller's apartment at Rosenheimer Straße 40. In the end, there were nine of them. In the fall of 1941, Nazi authorities began systematically deporting Jews to ghettos and camps in Eastern Europe.
Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels wrote in his diary: "The main thing is that the capital of the Reich be cleansed of Jews; and I will neither rest nor relent until this goal is fully achieved." The residents of Rosenheimer Straße were among those who were subsequently deported.
Remembering at the original site
Marie Rolshoven aims to honor the fate of these individuals. In 2016, she, along with her late mother and a friend, founded the initiative Denk Mal Am Ort (a wordplay meaning both "Think about it at the site" and "Memorial at the Site") inspired by the Amsterdam project Open Jewish Homes.
The idea is to invite people to the very location where everyday life once occurred. "You feel a strong connection to these individuals through the actual site," says Rolshoven. "It's different from visiting a memorial."
'My brother's bed used to be right here'
Two floors below, her neighbors had a similar experience. Denk Mal Am Ort found out that the Jewish Katzenellenbogen family had previously rented the apartment.
The family escaped Nazi Germany in 1939, just in time. "In 2018, 92-year-old Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen was invited back here, accompanied by his daughter, son-in-law, and grandson,” Rolshoven tells DW.
The Denk Mal Am Ort initiative discovered him through Facebook. Rolshoven recounts how touched the visitors were when the former resident walked in and remarked, "Yes, I remember it clearly. My brother's bed used to be right here. He was 10 when we had to leave the country."
Soon there will be no eyewitnesses left
Joel Ludwig Katzenellenbogen has since passed away, along with many other eyewitnesses. This highlights the importance of intergenerational remembrance, according to Rolshoven. She has already welcomed a descendant of a former resident into her home.
Claudia Samter's mother managed to escape from Berlin to Argentina, but her aunt was not as fortunate. Seeking assistance in tracing her family's history, Claudia contacted Denk Mal Am Ort. It turned out that her aunt had once been housed in Rolshoven's apartment.
Claudia Samter has already visited twice. "After all, there's no grave in a cemetery for her to visit," says Rolshoven. "We sat at the kitchen table to talk about life today and tomorrow, and we laughed a lot and cried, too. It felt good to give this space a new purpose once again."
Denk Mal Am Ort has so far organized 90 commemorative events in eight cities this year. Many young descendants attended, according to Rolshoven. "Knowing that they had stood in this stairwell and touched the same doorknob helped them."
Seeking traces of ancestors
19-year-old Adam Ethan Klein from Switzerland also wanted to learn more about his ancestors' history. "I always knew there was a story of escape, but it was never a significant topic at home,” he says.
"They'd say, ‘Yes, your great-grandparents left Germany in 1938, just in time. Luckily, otherwise you wouldn't be here today'."
Klein says his decision to dig deeper was prompted by the spread ofantisemitism, as well as the widespread slogan "Never again is now." (Editor's note: This slogan serves as a call to actively confront antisemitism, hatred, and threats to democracy today.)
The whole family was aware of a suitcase belonging to his maternal great-grandfather in the attic. However, no one ever looked inside until Adam finally opened the suitcase and discovered dozens of documents. He also found a letter from the Hanover District Court dated June 12, 1933, addressed to his great-grandfather, attorney Max Haas.
The letter stated: "As of today, following the decree issued by the Minister of Justice, you have been removed from the list of licensed attorneys."
'They were above all one thing: Jews'
Klein was profoundly affected by the letter: "With this single sentence, it became unmistakably clear to the families that they were not quite what they had aspired to be for generations: an average German family. From that moment on, they were above all one thing: Jews."
For Klein, this was a troubling realization. So was the news that someone had stabbed an ultra-Orthodox Jew to death in Zurich while shouting antisemitic slogans. The attack occurred not far from the synagogue where he had shortly before celebrated a cousin's bar mitzvah. (Editor's note: In Judaism, a bar mitzvah is a ceremony that marks a young person's coming of age in religious matters.)
"For the first time in my life, I felt that unsettling sensation of not quite belonging. Yet Zurich is my home, the city where I've lived carefree as a Jewish Swiss from birth," Adam would later write.
"That was definitely new, uncharted territory for me. I had always thought that such things don't happen in Switzerland. Maybe that was a bit naive of me," he admits.
The subject would not let him go. Adam continued his research, determined to write his high school graduation thesis about his relatives. In the spring of 2024, he set off with his parents, sister, grandmother, uncles, aunts and several cousins to visit the places where their ancestors had lived.
A magical encounter
At some point during their journey, they found themselves in Stuttgart, standing in front of a five-story building at Hölderlinstraße 55, when a man on a bike emerged from the courtyard and approached them.
"So, are you taking a guided tour of the city, or are you planning to move here?" he asked jokingly. The man was Thomas Koch, who had spent time researching the former residents of his house. When he heard the answer, "No, we're just checking out where our ancestors lived," he was thrilled.
Koch had already discovered that the former owners of the house, the Merzbacher brothers, sold it in 1936 for 75,000 Reichsmarks. From that amount, they had to pay 70,000 Reichsmarks in wealth taxes and the Reich Emigration Tax. The remaining sum was just enough to cover the ship fares to Brazil and the United States.
From 1937 to 1938, a family named Hirschheimer, who worked in the plywood trade, lived on the ground floor before they were forcibly relocated to a "Judenhaus." Their trail went cold in 1939, as Koch found no further records. So, he asked, "Are you the Hirschheimer family?" They were indeed.
Koch describes the encounter as magical. Adolf and Auguste Hirschheimer were Adam's great-great-grandparents, and their daughter, Ilse, was married to Max Haas.
Adam Klein and Thomas Koch have kept in touch since then. The next time Adam visited Stuttgart, he was invited over for coffee and cake.
Adam was impressed by the beautiful apartment. "It was fascinating to imagine how my ancestors once lived there, and it probably wasn't that different. Back then, there was likely coffee and cake as well."
Adam showed Koch photos of his grandmother, Ilse, who had married at the synagogue in Stuttgart, standing in the living room in her wedding gown. "In front of the door that we still have," says Koch.
“It was really moving to discover new roommates in a historical context set in the past. And I think this experience — this process of putting myself in their shoes — is a deeply empathetic one that simply brings us together through this apartment.”
Shattered identities
Ilse and Max Haas found refuge in England, while the Hirschheimers emigrated to Switzerland in 1939. Adolf Hirschheimer died in 1940 from a heart condition, but Adam, his great-great-grandson, believes he "certainly also died of a broken heart."
Auguste was brought to England by her son-in-law, Max, where the family felt homesick. "There, we were the Jews; here, we are the Germans. Try figuring that out," Ilse Haas wrote to a friend. Adam chose these lines as the title for his thesis.
Adam's great-grandparents could not find peace after being stripped of their homeland. From England, they eventually went to Israel and, at some point, returned to Europe — to Switzerland.
"At the end of their lives, my great-grandparents settled just a two-hour drive from their old homeland," Adam wrote. "When I look at their lives through the eyes of a great-grandson, it becomes clear that after breaking ties with Germany, they never managed to put down roots anywhere again."
"Remembering is important because, ultimately, we have to learn from history," says Adam. "And I think every single person has a responsibility— and the power — to actively keep memories alive. And hopefully, that can happen even without eyewitnesses.” For example, in his ancestors' former apartment.
This article was originally written in German.

title: Health Leaders Talk Expanding Access to Specialty Care
content:
When there are breakthrough technologies like xenotransplants, or novel cancer therapies, they’re transformative for diseases and conditions once thought incurable—but they can only save lives if the people that need them can access them. On September 10, TIME hosted the third annual TIME100 Health Leadership Forum in New York City, bringing together the TIME and TIME100 Health communities to discuss equity, longevity, and solution-driven care. The evening featured five expert panels, including The Access Gap: Expanding Pathways to Life-Saving Care. Moderated by TIME senior health correspondent Alice Park, the panel invited faculty physicians specializing in cell therapies from Oregon Health & Science University and Penn Medicine to take part in conversation with Amy Ronneberg, chief executive officer of NMDP, a global nonprofit connecting patients with lifesaving cell therapies and transplants. NMDP is a sponsor of the 2026 TIME100 Health Leadership Forum.
While modern science has solved some access issues, others still remain. “If we go back six years, the biggest barrier was the fact that there were not donors to match,” says Ronneberg. “As more patients have a donor, we now are facing issues around referral. Thousands of patients are not getting referred to transplant centers in a timely manner, those that are oftentimes are facing major barriers from a financial perspective.”
Dr. Eneida R. Nemecek, director of Pediatric Cell Therapy and Transplant & Cancer Clinical Research at Oregon Health & Science University, agreed that geography is a big problem for patients who need care. She said it’s a symptom of a bigger problem with the way our health systems have been designed. “When we're designing systems for healthcare, we forget that we're designing the systems for the patient. The system designs the system for itself, and then we try to adjust it to the patient,” Nemecek says.
Because of how specialized CAR-T therapies were designed and tested, there can be natural bottlenecks when it comes to scaling up and disseminating it to a wider audience. Dr. David L. Porter, director of the Center for Cell Therapy and Transplant at Penn Medicine, says that advanced therapies like bone marrow transplants or cellular immunotherapies are developed and largely performed at major academic institutions in big cities, usually as a proof of concept. However, swaths of the population in the country do not live near one of these institutions or have to drive hours to one that has both the technology and the expertise. Now, there are seven FDA-approved commercial CAR-T cells, and the manufacturers have no problem receiving cells from collection centers, manufacturing them, and returning them. “The barrier is actually collecting the cells,” Porter says. “It's a very specialized process.”
Additionally, undergoing collection and treatment causes huge displacement in patients and their caregivers’ lives. The entire process of treatment and testing can take weeks. “We have those discussions all the time that people would accept suboptimal therapy and give up the potential for curative therapy because they can’t do that,” Porter says. “There are an enormous number of initiatives trying to improve, and they move the needle a little bit.” One of these methods is to try to give these therapies in community health centers closer to where the patients are. Porter and his colleagues recently conducted a pilot study at the University of Pennsylvania with two of their community partners to implement high-end CAR-T cell therapy in a community setting. Over the course of about a year, they’ve been able to treat over 60 patients who otherwise largely would not have had access because they would not have traveled to a big city for it.
With science changing fast and treatment outcomes improving, Ronneberg says that it’s more important than ever to “get the education and awareness out to the community,” and provide them with “funds to travel.” As a cancer survivor herself, Ronneberg recalled having a hard time navigating the process even when she had everything at her fingertips—a husband who’s a doctor, resources from her job at the NMDP. The organization’s focus has moved beyond simply finding donors to now getting patients to the right treatment they need at the right locations, whether that’s an academic center or a community center.
To this end, Nemecek and her colleagues have been working on projects like ACCESS Initiative, in partnership with NMDP, in order to start training community centers and equip them with accreditation needed to collect cells. “With valuable telehealth, with use of technology,” Nemecek says, “that’s really where the future of our field is.”
The TIME100 Health Leadership Forum was presented by the American Cancer Society, Kite—a Gilead Sciences company, Insulet, Musely, and NMDP.

title: The ‘father of Malaysia from Sabah’, through his son’s eyes
content:
“You couldn’t just not turn up,” his son, Asgari Stephens, told FMT Lifestyle with a smile.
That ritual spoke volumes: the statesman who spent his days among crowds still made time to keep his family close.
There were also picnics and days by the sea. “He was a very loving dad. Sometimes, I don’t know how he managed to do so much,” added Asgari, 66.
Born on Sept 14, 1920, in Kudat, Sabah, Fuad would have turned 106 just two days before Malaysia Day this year.
Known as the “father of Malaysia from Sabah”, he played a key role in the negotiations leading to Malaysia’s formation and became Sabah’s first chief minister.
But to Asgari, he was simply a doting parent who prized education and taught his children honesty and the importance of giving back.
Fuad’s warmth reached well beyond the home, allowing him to connect just as easily with villagers as with heads of state.
Fluent in Malay, English and several Chinese dialects – and having even picked up Japanese during World War II – he put his gift for languages to use by helping others write letters to the authorities in English.
Of Eurasian-Kadazan heritage, he and his family converted to Islam in 1971. The Kadazan community remained close to his heart, and they embraced him as their “Huguan Siou” (paramount leader).
“In his will, he included his best wishes for the Kadazan people. It always makes me very emotional,” said Asgari, a veteran venture capitalist and angel investor.
Yet Fuad’s hopes for Sabah crossed ethnic lines. “I always like to think he was a guy who believed in multiracial politics,” Asgari added, saying he believes his father envisioned a more inclusive, meritocratic Sabah that developed the skills of its people.
At the same time, he did not want Sabah to gain independence only to remain heavily dependent on the old colonial structures. “We had very few graduates, and the government machinery was still run by the British.”
Still, his father was initially cautious about the idea of Malaysia. “Without a united front – Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore acting together as a counterweight – we would really have been quite lost, and I think that was his concern.”
According to Asgari, it was Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew who played a key role in convincing Fuad to support the formation of Malaysia.
“He was very good friends with Lee. They had been through the formation of Malaysia together, sitting on committees to decide how they would participate and join Malaysia as partners.”
Singapore’s departure on Aug 9, 1965, broke his father’s heart. The following day, he wrote Lee a letter, a copy of which was discovered decades later by Asgari’s sister, Faridah.
“I feel like death. Tears, heartbreak, completely lost and betrayed,” Fuad wrote, mourning the years spent “selling the idea of Malaysia to my people”.
Then, on June 6, 1976, tragedy struck. The aircraft carrying Fuad, his eldest son Johari and nine others crashed in Kota Kinabalu, killing everyone aboard. It became known as the “Double Six” tragedy.
Fuad had been 55 and only weeks into his second term as Sabah’s chief minister. Several of the state’s ministers also died in the crash, deepening the state’s loss.
At boarding school in Australia, Asgari was told by his housemaster early the next morning that his father and brother had died.
For about five years, he said, a “black cloud” hung over those left behind, and family time once filled with beaches, boats and laughter became painfully quiet.
Asked what his father would think of Sabah today, Asgari reckons he would say “it’s a big shame”.
“We were one of the richest states, and now we are one of the poorest. After so many years of independence, I think it’s shocking. Given the resources that we’ve had, it shouldn’t have been like this.”
Still, he sees traces of his father’s belief in a multiracial Sabah in the way people of different backgrounds continue to mix freely.
“I hope that Sabah’s politicians can come together and really act for all Sabahans. I’ve been feeling optimistic more recently,” Asgari said.
For him, Malaysia Day brings pride in his father’s legacy, tempered by sadness over what might have been.
“If Singapore hadn’t left, if my father had not passed away, things might have been different. I like to think they might have been different,” he concluded.

title: Africa: Global Initiative Launched to Improve Access to Mpox Vaccines
content:
A global initiative to establish a stockpile of mpox vaccines was launched on 27 August, creating a long-term mechanism to ensure countries have access to vaccines when responding to mpox outbreaks.
Set to begin operations later this month, this new global mpox vaccine stockpile that all countries can access is a resource that was approved by the Board of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi) in 2025, and is funded by Gavi and coordinated by the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision. The ICG partners are the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) and the World Health Organization (WHO).
The initiative builds on the Access and Allocation Mechanism established in 2024 during the last mpox Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC), and will ensure that countries have timely and equitable access to vaccines for outbreak response.
Mpox continues to cause outbreaks globally, with two-thirds of reported cases occurring in the African Region. From 1 January 2022 to 31 July 2026, 145 countries and territories reported 190 683 confirmed cases and 529 deaths. Mpox is a viral disease that spreads primarily through close physical contact between people, while animal-to-human transmission continues to occur in parts of Africa, contributing to the ongoing risk of new outbreaks. Mpox can cause severe disease, especially in children and people with suppressed immune systems. By protecting people at risk of infection and severe disease, vaccines help contain mpox outbreaks more quickly, prevent severe illness and save lives.
Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn
Quotes from partners:
Dr Sania Nishtar, CEO of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, said: "During the 2022 mpox outbreak, lower-income countries were left behind when it came to access to vaccines and it was clear that a mechanism was needed to ensure this global public good could be accessed by those who need it most. Core to the Gavi Leap approach is increasing our responsiveness to country needs, and the bottom line is that any country in the world - not just those with the ability to pay the most - should be able to use this tool to save lives. That is why Gavi supported the international response to the 2024 global mpox emergency by securing rapid access to doses through our First Response Fund, and why our Board agreed to establish and finance a global stockpile managed by our ICG partners. Our hope is that this stockpile will keep the world safer from the threat of this deadly disease."
Jagan Chapagain, Secretary General and CEO of the IFRC, said: "Mpox is a horrible illness so I'm pleased that we've got to this important step in the battle to control it. Access to vaccines - for all who need them - is absolutely vital. That's why this global coordination mechanism and vaccine stockpile matters. Both will help ensure vaccines reach the people and communities at greatest risk - when and where they are needed most. This is rare good news."
Dr Daniela Garone, International Medical Coordinator, MSF, said: "MSF welcomes the establishment of a global mpox vaccine stockpile under the International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision, a mechanism that allows for the equal allocation of vaccines as based on demand and impact in controlling disease outbreaks. The distinctive nature of mpox, with the coexistence of different variants that affect different populations, now demands a close collaboration between country, regional and global mechanisms as well as between disease programmes, health managers, communities and public health partners to reach more people with mpox vaccines."
Catherine Russell, UNICEF Executive Director, said: "Mpox can be devastating for children - not just its physical effects, but also the stigma, interrupted learning, and fear that can come with being isolated from family and friends. This vital initiative will help us quickly get vaccines to the children, families, and communities most at risk of the disease."
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, said: "The launch of a stockpile of mpox vaccines is an important step towards a more sustainable and equitable approach to mpox outbreak response. By establishing a dedicated global stockpile, using an approach that has proven successful for managing other emergency vaccines, we are ensuring that countries can access them more quickly when they need them, saving lives and containing outbreaks before they spread further."
Note to editors
Mpox
Mpox is a viral illness that spreads mainly through close physical contact, including sexual contact. The disease can be debilitating and disfiguring, affecting men, women and children in different contexts, and can, in some cases, lead to severe complications and death. WHO Mpox factsheet
International Coordinating Group (ICG) on Vaccine Provision
The ICG was established in 1997, following major outbreaks of meningitis in Africa, as a mechanism to manage and coordinate the provision of emergency vaccine supplies and antibiotics to countries during major outbreaks. Although the occurrence of outbreaks is often unpredictable, further disease spread can be controlled by timely vaccination.
The core mandate of the ICG is to make available and ensure equitable access to licensed vaccines for cholera, meningitis, yellow fever, and Ebola virus disease during outbreaks.
The ICG mechanism seeks to ensure timely and targeted deployment of vaccines so that they can be used effectively in emergency settings where they are most needed.
The ICG manages the global emergency vaccine stockpiles and, working with partners, donors, and manufacturers, determines their size and composition with the goal of ensuring that adequate stocks of emergency supplies are accessible for emergency response.
In 2024, WHO and partners created the ad hoc Access and Allocation Mechanism for mpox vaccines. The longer term ICG will continue the work initiated under the AAM.
In 2025, the Gavi Board formally approved the establishment and financing of the global mpox vaccine stockpile. under the long-standing ICG mechanism to include mpox.

title: The ‘troubled’ class assignment that changed Lee’s teaching career
content:
The ‘troubled’ class assignment that changed Lee’s teaching career
When Lee Casuscelli got her first job out of teachers college in the 1980s, she was given what might be termed a challenging first assignment at The Grange Public School in south-west Sydney.
“She just got given the troubled class, I guess they called it, and no teacher really was able to do anything with these kids,” says her daughter Lauren Casuscelli. “They couldn’t really sit still at the start, they were jumping out of the windows and it was a bit chaotic.”
But Lauren says her mother gave her students 100 per cent of her focus. Attendance soon improved, the class became much more settled, and students were able to learn. “She just saw them as kids, not their disability,” Lauren says.
That class at The Grange Public about 40 years ago would become the first step in a long and dedicated career working to improve the lives of students with disabilities and autism.
When Casuscelli died suddenly in a car crash in February, it prompted an outpouring of grief in the Camden community and across the state.
Local MP Sally Quinnell told NSW parliament that hundreds of parents had paid their respects to Casuscelli, describing how she had “helped their children to grow and how she supported families with children with additional needs”.
That legacy was honoured on Tuesday at Parliament House in Canberra at an event held by Schools Plus, an education not-for-profit, with the inaugural Lee Casuscelli Excellence in Special Education Award.
Early in Casuscelli’s career, understanding of autism was much more limited both in schools and the general community. She developed numerous programs and initiatives to support students with autism.
One of those programs was called Tool Time, which she established at Our Lady Help of Christians in Rosemeadow in the 2000s. In one-hour classes, she helped equip specific groups – such as teen boys – with practical tools to navigate the world.
The junior group would cover topics such as how to make a friend, how to keep a friend, and the sorts of social skills people with autism might struggle with. There was also advice for their parents.
She went on to become the principal of Aspect Western Sydney School and Aspect Macarthur School before joining Schools Plus as its director of education.
The inaugural winner of the award is Dr Dawn Grant-Skiba, principal of Warrah Specialist School in Dural. The $50,000 prize includes $20,000 for a teacher fellowship, which is 12 months of professional development, including national networking and master classes.
A further $30,000 will enable Warrah Specialist School to expand innovative approaches that improve outcomes for students with disability and diverse learning needs.
Schools Plus chief executive Sherrill Nixon said: “We are delighted to recognise Dawn, whose work reflects so many of the values Lee held so strongly.”
Grant-Skiba, who was born in Jamaica, has worked across mainstream and specialist support schools in her 26-year teaching career. She says an early experience as a 12-year-old helping older women in her community learn to write their names and develop basic numeracy skillis has been a strong influence.
“The ability to do that has changed their lives,” she says.
She said while she was happy to teach students who learnt easily, she got the most joy from students who needed her more. “My creative juices flow, I get excited when they read a word, when before, they couldn’t recognise a letter.
“Those formative years really inspired me when I did come into teaching, to always look for the underdogs that others didn’t see as much.”

Alban-Udi community representative shares impressions of Ganjasar Monastery visit
content:
Alban-Udi community representative shares impressions of Ganjasar Monastery visit
- 21 September, 2026
- 18:16
Rafig Danakari, Deputy Chairman of the Alban-Udi Christian Religious Community, who visited the Ganjasar Monastery in Vangli village of the Aghdara district, shared his impressions of the visit.
According to the Public Relations Department of the Reconstruction, Construction and Management Service in Khankandi city, Aghdara and Khojaly districts, Danakari told Report that the visit of members of the Alban-Udi community to the Ganjasar Monastery after many years was of particular significance.
"We are very happy to be here today. As a result of the liberation of our lands, we can now come to this sacred place freely. For many years, for 100-200 years, we could not come here. Today, we prayed for the souls of our martyrs, commemorated their memory, and lit candles. May God rest the souls of all our martyrs.
Today is also significant for us from another perspective. It is the birthday of the Virgin Mary. Being at the Ganjasar Monastery on this special day has a special meaning for us. We want to continue regularly visiting Ganjasar Monastery, as well as churches and monasteries located in other regions of Azerbaijan, pray here, and light candles," he said.
Danakari stressed that it is also important to introduce these historical sites to the international community:
"Because these are our history and our cultural and religious heritage. We want the whole world to see that the historical heritage of Caucasian Albania is still being preserved today."

title: In Perù hanno rimesso in funzione i waru waru inca: 3.000 anni dopo aiutano ancora le patate contro il clima estremo
content:
In Perù hanno rimesso in funzione i waru waru inca: 3.000 anni dopo aiutano ancora le patate contro il clima estremo
Indice
Hanno rialzato la terra, scavato di nuovo i canali e rimesso le patate dove questo sistema le aveva protette per secoli. Ad Acora, nel dipartimento peruviano di Puno, sulle pianure dell’altopiano che circondano il lago Titicaca, le comunità aymara hanno recuperato cinque waru waru. La prima campagna agricola 2025-2026 è già arrivata al raccolto: patate native da mangiare, conservare come seme, trasformare in chuño e tunta e, quando avanzano, vendere.
Il progetto condotto nell’ultimo anno da World Monuments Fund Perú insieme all’Asociación Aymara Suma Yapu ha riportato in produzione una tecnologia agricola che la FAO fa risalire a circa 3.000 anni fa. Più che un reperto archeologico, è un sistema idraulico ancora perfettamente comprensibile: campi rialzati, acqua intorno, gravità e una conoscenza molto precisa del clima locale.
Il campo si alza, l’acqua resta nei canali
Un waru waru assomiglia a una grande aiuola agricola sollevata rispetto al terreno circostante. Tra una piattaforma e l’altra corrono canali capaci di raccogliere e distribuire l’acqua. Una geometria semplice che, vista dall’alto, può creare disegni spettacolari e che sul terreno svolge parecchio lavoro sporco: drena quando l’acqua è troppa, conserva umidità quando manca e modifica il microclima intorno alle colture. La stessa municipalità di Acora descrive questi campi come una forma tradizionale di adattamento alle pianure alluvionali del Titicaca.
C’è poi una specie di riscaldamento passivo incorporato nel paesaggio. Durante il giorno l’acqua nei canali assorbe calore; quando la temperatura precipita durante la notte, ne restituisce una parte, contribuendo a smorzare il gelo intorno alle piante. È un meccanismo documentato dalla FAO nei sistemi agricoli andini. Ad Acora siamo oltre i 3.800 metri di quota, dove siccità, gelate e forti escursioni termiche non sono precisamente inconvenienti marginali.
Anche il fango ha il suo mestiere. Sedimenti, alghe e materia organica si accumulano sul fondo dei canali e possono essere recuperati e riportati sui campi come materiale ricco di nutrienti. Acqua, terra e residui tornano così nello stesso ciclo produttivo senza bisogno di trasformare il paesaggio in una macchina particolarmente complicata. La sofisticazione, qui, sta tutta nel sapere dove scavare e come gestire ciò che c’è già.
Le patate raccolte diventano cibo, semi e scorta per i mesi difficili
Durante il primo ciclo dei cinque waru waru recuperati, le comunità hanno puntato soprattutto sulle patate native. Una parte del raccolto è rimasta alle famiglie e una parte è stata conservata per le semine successive. Altri tuberi sono diventati chuño e tunta, due sistemi tradizionali di conservazione che sfruttano proprio il freddo dell’altopiano. Il chuño è ottenuto disidratando le patate attraverso gelo e asciugatura; la tunta, di colore chiaro, prevede anche ripetuti congelamenti e permanenza in acqua corrente prima dell’essiccazione.
Il vantaggio è molto concreto: una parte del raccolto può essere conservata molto più a lungo rispetto alla patata fresca. E quello che supera i bisogni delle famiglie entra nel mercato locale, trasformando il recupero del waru waru anche in una piccola fonte di reddito. Alla fine di agosto, circa quattro tonnellate di patate native coltivate nei campi recuperati sono state portate a Lima da rappresentanti di quattro comunità di Acora per essere vendute, scambiate e utilizzate in degustazioni.
Il lavoro riguarda anche ciò che rischia di scomparire molto prima dei campi: la diversità delle sementi. Il Centro Internacional de la Papa (CIP) e MATER partecipano allo studio delle varietà di patate native coltivate dalle comunità, mettendo insieme conservazione genetica, conoscenze agricole e utilizzi alimentari. Nel territorio del Titicaca la diversità della patata è una faccenda tutt’altro che ornamentale: significa avere varietà con caratteristiche differenti davanti a freddo, siccità, suoli e tempi di maturazione diversi.
Il cambiamento climatico ha rimesso un sistema antico nell’elenco delle soluzioni utili
Nel 2025 i campi waru waru di Puno sono entrati nel World Monuments Watch, insieme a 24 altri luoghi culturali considerati vulnerabili o particolarmente importanti per le comunità che li custodiscono. La candidatura era stata presentata da Suma Yapu, associazione guidata da donne indigene, insieme alla Direzione decentrata della Cultura di Puno. Il Ministero della Cultura peruviano li ha indicati espressamente come patrimonio capace di contribuire alla resilienza e alla sicurezza alimentare nel contesto della crisi climatica.
Il recupero di Acora si inserisce poi nel programma globale Cultivating Resilience di WMF, dedicato proprio a paesaggi storici che conservano forme tradizionali di adattamento ambientale. Qui il patrimonio culturale ha una caratteristica abbastanza comoda: si può mangiare. E continua a funzionare soltanto finché qualcuno conserva semi, pulisce canali, ricostruisce piattaforme e tramanda il modo corretto di farlo.
I waru waru, infatti, difficilmente possono essere trattati come una tecnologia da esportare in blocco e montare altrove. La FAO sottolinea quanto questi sistemi richiedano conoscenze specifiche, manutenzione e lavoro collettivo. La loro forza nasce proprio dall’adattamento a un territorio preciso e da generazioni di prove fatte sul campo, con pochissimo spazio per il manuale d’istruzioni universale.
Ad Acora, però, cinque di quei campi sono tornati a produrre. Dopo tremila anni di siccità, gelate, abbandoni e ritorni, l’ultima innovazione agricola dell’altopiano peruviano ha ancora canali pieni d’acqua e patate sotto terra. Solo che è parecchio più vecchia di quanto suggerisca la parola “innovazione”.

title: FOVISSSTE liquida adeudos de 326 mil acreditados y retomará la construcción de vivienda tras 34 años
content:
FOVISSSTE liquida adeudos de 326 mil acreditados y retomará la construcción de vivienda tras 34 años
El director general del ISSSTE, Martí Batres, informó que el Programa de Justicia Social ha atendido a la mayoría de las carteras vencidas y anunció la edificación de 200 mil casas con tiendas SUPERISSSTE en todo el país.
El Fondo de la Vivienda del Instituto de Seguridad y Servicios Sociales de los Trabajadores del Estado (FOVISSSTE) perdonó adeudos, aplicó liquidaciones y brindó esquemas de apoyo financiero a un total de 326 mil derechohabientes cuyos créditos resultaban impagables. En un acto de entrega de 519 constancias de finiquito a beneficiarios de la Ciudad de México, el director general del ISSSTE, Martí Batres Guadarrama, garantizó la certeza patrimonial de las y los trabajadores: "Sus deudas están canceladas, sus deudas están terminadas. El FOVISSSTE se hizo para el trabajador, la trabajadora. Hoy se les entrega su vivienda. Eso es lo más importante de todo, ya son dueños de su vivienda a partir de este momento. Se trataba de rescatar al FOVISSSTE y se está logrando".
Al inicio de la administración federal, el diagnóstico de la cartera de crédito reveló que la mitad de las 800 mil financiaciones activas presentaban graves complicaciones administrativas e incrementos exorbitantes en los saldos. Sobre este diagnóstico y la atención pendiente para el resto de los afectados, Batres Guadarrama precisó los alcances del programa: "Encontramos que aquí, en FOVISSSTE, de los 800 mil créditos, 400 mil tenían problemas y muchos de ellos eran francamente impagables. En este momento se ha ayudado ya a poco más de 326 mil, o sea, nos quedan todavía 74 mil a los que vamos a ayudar también con condonaciones".
Además de los esquemas de reestructuración crediticia, el organismo asistencial alista un giro operativo para volver a edificar soluciones habitacionales de forma directa después de más de tres décadas de inactividad constructora. Respecto al plan que contempla la creación de 200 mil inmuebles residenciales en la República Mexicana, el titular del instituto destacó: "Después de 34 años, el Fondo retomará esta tarea con la edificación de 200 mil viviendas en todo el país, como parte de las acciones del Segundo Piso de la Cuarta Transformación", añadiendo que cada uno de los desarrollos habitacionales incorporará un establecimiento de la red SUPERISSSTE.
Esta nueva faceta institucional busca mitigar el rezago habitacional concentrándose de manera prioritaria en las familias y trabajadores con menor nivel de percepción salarial. Al respecto, la vocal ejecutiva del FOVISSSTE, Jabnely Maldonado Meza, fundamentó el retorno de la capacidad constructiva del organismo: "Recuperamos una atribución fundamental para que el precio de la vivienda sea asequible. Construir vivienda para sus trabajadores, que sea vivienda barata, segura, que esté habitable, que esté bien organizada. Esa es la tarea que acabamos de recobrar en semanas pasadas gracias a esta iniciativa de nuestra Presidenta".
Durante la jornada en la capital del país, las 519 cancelaciones de hipoteca beneficiaron a trabajadores residentes de las alcaldías Cuauhtémoc, Iztacalco y Venustiano Carranza. Sobre los montos cancelados a las familias mediante este esquema de bienestar social, Maldonado Meza detalló que la condonación alcanzó pasivos "de hasta un millón 200 mil pesos", garantizando el derecho a la vivienda adecuada que promueve el Gobierno de México.

title: Oxford University approves return of 39 Naga ancestral remains from UK museum
content:
Oxford University approves return of 39 Naga ancestral remains from UK museum
Oxford University Council has approved the return of 39 Naga ancestral remains held at the Pitt Rivers Museum, with repatriation expected by year-end.
The University of Oxford Council has approved the repatriation of 39 Naga ancestral human remains held at the Pitt Rivers Museum (PRM) in the UK, marking a major step towards returning remains taken during the colonial era to their homeland.
The repatriation, which is expected to be completed by the end of this year, would bring closure to an initiative undertaken jointly by the Forum for Naga Reconciliation (FNR) and its Recover Restore and Decolonise (RRaD), along with Naga tribe bodies.
In a letter to FNR convener Wati Aier, PRM director Laura Van Broekhoven conveyed that the University’s Council had on July 13 formally agreed to return 39 human remains while declining the repatriation of one set as it does not have clear evidence that it was of Naga origin. The letter expressed hope that work can now commence towards bringing the Naga ancestors to their homeland.
“The path home for the Naga ancestors has now become a reality as they journey to the Naga homeland. Repatriation, for the Nagas, is not simply about bones and ancestral remains finding their way back to the land, but importantly it is about memory returning to where it belongs. It is an essential step of a longer journey towards justice and dignity, and towards healing and wholeness,” read a joint statement of the FNR-RRaD and Naga tribe bodies.
Also Read: Naga delegation seek return of ancestral remains from UK’s Pitt Rivers Museum
The Pitt Rivers Museum reportedly holds over 6,000 Naga artefacts. A member of RRaD informed that while the museum is open to welcoming Naga researchers to study those collections, reclaiming them is not the RRaD’s focus presently.
Angami Public Organisation (APO) president Thejao Vihienuo said the matter of the burial of the Naga ancestral remains after their repatriation is being pursued with the state government, with the hope of giving them a dignified burial.
Altogether, around 219 Naga ancestral human remains are said to be under the care of the PRM.
“The Naga ancestral remains were taken away under duress during colonial era by colonial administrators and collectors,” coordinator of RRaD Ellen Konyak Jamir had earlier told HT.
“The knowledge that our ancestral remains are exhibited in museums across the world, or they are boxed up, housed in museums, and they are treated as specimens and collectibles; that has been news for us, and we have all been very shocked to know about this. So we (RRaD team) have tried our best as a team to go out to our community to share and talk about this information. This is a community-led initiative,” she said.
A Naga delegation visited the UK in 2025 on the invitation of the PRM to strengthen the repatriation process. The team also met with representatives from various British museums that held Naga belongings and human remains. The museums in the UK that hold Naga artefacts and remains taken away from Naga communities during the colonial rule include the British Museum, Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology at Cambridge University, Manchester University, South Asia Gallery, Horniman Museum and Bristol Museum.

title: 500+ Tonnes of Waste Removed: How These Volunteers Clean Himachal’s Himalayan Trails
content: Every year, as pilgrims and trekkers visit Himachal Pradesh’s high-altitude trails, the mountains silently absorb the weight of human presence. When the snow melts and the festivals are over, it reveals more than alpine meadows and sacred landscapes. Discarded plastic, food wrappers, clothes, and abandoned gear surface along fragile routes, turning places of spiritual and ecological significance into unintended dumping grounds. As visitor footfall increases, the burden on these Himalayan ecosystems grows heavier. For RP Negi Yullam, Founder of the Himalayn Tribe Foundation, the problem became impossible to ignore during his early visits to places like Shrikhand Mahadev and Kinnaur Kailash. He saw plastic buried under snow, offerings left behind, and no system to carry waste back. That raised a question: if these are places that people choose to walk through for pilgrimage and adventure, could they also become part of the effort to protect them? It was within this intersection of travel, faith and environmental strain that the Himalayn Tribe Foundation emerged as a grassroots collective working to restore, protect, preserve and reimagine how people move through some of the Indian Himalayas’ most sensitive pilgrimage and trekking corridors. The moment that started it “Himalayn Tribe Foundation’s work had to exist because the Himalayas were silently paying the price of devotion and adventure,” says RP Negi Yullam. “During early visits to places like Shrikhand Mahadev and Kinnaur Kailash, I saw plastic buried under snow, offerings left behind, and no system to carry waste back. That moment made it clear that authorities alone cannot protect such remote terrains. Those who walk these sacred and fragile routes must also take responsibility.” Himalayn Tribe Foundation is a grassroots organisation currently working in Himachal Pradesh to address environmental degradation, waste mismanagement and community welfare in ecologically sensitive pilgrimage and trekking routes. The surge in pilgrimage and trekking footfall has brought with it an accumulation of waste that fragile ecosystems are ill-equipped to manage. These trails are not just environmentally significant; they also hold strong cultural and spiritual meaning for local communities. For RP Negi, that made involving the people who travel through these landscapes particularly important. “People who trek or go on pilgrimage directly interact with the ecosystem. When conservation is led by those who walk these trails, the connection becomes personal, not instructional,” he explains. “At high altitudes, even a small wrapper can remain for decades. When travellers participate in cleanups, they don’t just remove waste — they return home with awareness. That behavioural shift is the strongest form of conservation.” Instead of asking people to care, they got them involved Himalayn Tribe Foundation is a grassroots organisation currently working in Himachal Pradesh to address environmental degradation, waste mismanagement and community welfare in ecologically sensitive pilgrimage and trekking routes. Its approach is community-driven. Instead of positioning conservation as an external intervention, the foundation encourages trekkers and pilgrims to participate as volunteers, creating a shared sense of responsibility. Over the last three years, Sujal Chauhan, a core team member of the foundation, has participated in almost all its clean-up drives at higher-altitude pilgrimage and trekking routes. The foundation currently works across multiple high-altitude and culturally significant routes in Himachal Pradesh. Its major clean-up drives are conducted at Shrikhand Mahadev, Kinnaur Kailash, Yula Kanda and Rani Kanda. It has also worked around Bhimakali Temple, Sarahan Bushahr and nearby villages. Alongside clean-up drives, the foundation is involved in solid waste management initiatives in Rampur Bushahr, plantation drives, heritage restoration and winter relief initiatives, including clothing distribution for local communities. Over the years, the Foundation says it has removed more than 500 tonnes of waste from Himalayan trekking and pilgrimage routes. It conducts eight major clean-up drives every year across several high-altitude routes. These include Kinnaur Kailash twice a year, Yula Kanda twice a year, Rani Kanda once a year, Baba Pass once a year, Shrikhand Mahadev twice a year and Manimahesh once a year. Each drive typically involves 15–20 volunteers, supported by two groups led by regular NGO team members who coordinate and conduct the campaigns. The work extends beyond physically removing waste. The Foundation also conducts environmental awareness campaigns among pilgrims, trekkers, local communities and visitors, encouraging them to think about what they carry into these fragile landscapes and what they leave behind. In recent years, the foundation also began collaborating with government bodies and local administrations to expand the scale of its work, signalling a shift from informal action to structured, long-term environmental stewardship. The waste has to come down on their backs The clean-up, however, is far from simple. At high altitude, there are no roads, bins or vehicles waiting to carry the waste away. Volunteers have to collect, segregate and carry it down themselves. For some volunteers, the experience changes how they see the mountains themselves. “A cleanup drive begins days before the trek with planning, permissions and volunteer briefings,” says Sujal. “On the trail, we move slowly, collecting waste while adapting to altitude, weather and terrain. Every item is segregated and carried down manually, often on our backs, especially from trek routes like Shrikhand Mahadev, which is 35 kilometres one side.” At such heights, even basic tasks can become physically demanding. “The hardest part is logistics. At high altitudes, there are no roads, bins or vehicles. Even on difficult treks, heavy waste is carried down by volunteers,” Sujal explains. “Weather can change suddenly at high altitudes, oxygen levels drop, and safety is always a concern. Also, managing mixed waste like plastic, glass and religious offerings is complex. People see the final cleanup photos, but not the physical exhaustion and planning behind them.” The drive, he says, ends only when the waste is handed over to proper disposal points. When a pilgrimage becomes a clean-up mission For some volunteers, the experience changes how they see the mountains themselves. For Bhuvan Malik from Kota, Rajasthan, volunteering felt like giving back to a place that had given him so much. “The Himalayas offer peace, adventure and spirituality, but they also suffer silently,” he says. “Joining a cleanup drive transformed the journey from consumption to contribution. Instead of just taking photos, we became part of the solution. It made the experience more meaningful and humbling.” What he saw during one of the clean-ups brought the scale of the problem home. “Finding plastic bottles and footwear near glaciers and sacred sites was shocking. In Shrikhand Mahadev, the sacred Parvati Kund was full of clothes like underwear dumped in the corner. Many other sacred sites have the same problem,” he says. Seeing waste frozen into snow at extreme altitudes made the volunteers realise how permanent their impact could be. “Carrying that waste down ourselves changed how we travel forever,” Bhuvan says. “Now, we pack consciously, avoid disposables and encourage others to do the same. The mountains taught us to be responsible.” For the foundation, that behavioural change is as important as the waste collected. The people living here are joining too The shift is not limited to trekkers and pilgrims. The foundation says the response within local communities is changing too. Anchal Negi, a local community member from Kinnaur, recalls that residents were initially sceptical of the clean-up drives. “Initially, many locals were sceptical, and clean-ups were seen as temporary efforts,” she says. But repeated efforts have gradually changed that attitude. In places like Yulla Kanda, Kinnaur Kailash and Shrikhand Mahadev, people now recognise the foundation and ask how they can help. “Now, villagers inform us about waste hotspots and sometimes join the drives themselves. In places like Sarahan and local villages, participation has grown, especially among youth.” For local residents, cleaner routes are increasingly being connected to both tourism and cultural pride. “Locals now understand that cleaner routes benefit tourism and cultural pride. The foundation has helped turn concern into collective responsibility,” Anchal says. The real goal isn't just cleaner trails — it is responsible travellers RP Negi believes the foundation’s efforts are working because the biggest change is behavioural. “Over the past three years, we’ve seen pilgrims asking where to dispose of the waste, locals joining drives, and repeat visitors carrying trash back themselves,” he says. In places like Yulla Kanda, Kinnaur Kailash and Shrikhand Mahadev, people now recognise the foundation and ask how they can help. Alongside the clean-up drives, the Foundation’s environmental awareness campaigns among pilgrims, trekkers, local communities and visitors are helping reinforce this shift — taking the message of responsible travel beyond the people who directly participate in clean-ups. “That shift from indifference to participation tells us this effort is working,” says RP Negi. “Awareness at ground level grows slowly, but it stays.” And perhaps that is the larger change the foundation is trying to create. The goal is not simply to remove the waste already lying on the trails, but to change the way people understand their presence in the mountains — whether they arrive for faith, adventure or both. When pilgrims and trekkers begin carrying their waste back, when locals report waste hotspots and when volunteers return home more conscious of what they carry into fragile landscapes, conservation stops being someone else’s responsibility. It becomes part of the journey itself.

title: Even after her death, Hana Razga is the glue that keeps her family together
content:
Hana Marta Razga: Feminist. Advocate. Mentor. Community builder. Born May 28, 1947, in London; died Jan 31, 2026, in Edmonton; died of sepsis; aged 78.
Imagine what it must have been like to wake up in Prague on Aug. 21, 1968 when, overnight, thousands of Soviet tanks rolled into Czechoslovakia to extinguish the brief liberalization period known as the Prague Spring.
For 21-year-old Hana Marta Razga, it was a turning point. She left her homeland along with her fiancé Jan Soukup, to courageously forge a new life in Canada, knowing that she might never return home to see her family again.
Born in London to Czechoslovak diplomats, Hana was the fifth of seven children. She lived in England and Hungary, as well as Czechoslovakia as a child. It was an unusual upbringing that exposed her to other cultures, languages and political systems.
By the end of 1968, Hana and Jan had arrived in Canada. They were married in Banff in the spring of 1969 and shortly afterward, settled in Edmonton to start a family. They had four children: Katarina, Jana, Olivia and Alex, before they separated in 1988.
Hana made sure that her children received equal attention and resources. Having four children spread quite far apart in age meant that she was always managing a wide range of interests and demands. She created a monthly “Day Out” where she would take one child out for lunch and shopping for new clothes or toys, on a rotating schedule. This was her opportunity for one-on-one time. It was a day that made each child feel special, seen and heard.
Hana spent her life advocating for fairness and social justice in Canada. She championed women and children throughout her career, her political engagement and her volunteer work. She lived simply and deliberately, mindful of her environmental impact long before “global warming” became a household term. Hana’s dedication to conservation however showed up in quirky ways. Birthday cards arrived with messages written on sticky notes so the card could be reused. And she insisted on flushing her toilet with cold bath water left in the tub.
In 1983, Hana was hired at Transport Canada to create opportunities for women. Her female colleagues became lifelong friends and these feminists helped establish Edmonton’s Canada Place Child Care Society so mothers who worked for the government could have their children cared for in the same building. The centre still operates, over 35 years later.
When Hana retired from public service, she shared her pension with her two unmarried sisters in the Czech Republic. She also began running as an NDP candidate in numerous federal, provincial and municipal campaigns in Conservative Alberta years before the historic NDP win in 2015.
Hana invested thousands of dollars of her own money and countless hours door-knocking to meet constituents. She was deeply disappointed with each loss but she kept coming back because she held a steadfast conviction to her ideals and values. She was stubborn and in it to win.
She volunteered with the Big Brothers Big Sisters of Edmonton, located in what would become her beloved neighbourhood of Riverdale, on the banks of the North Saskatchewan River. She had a deep respect for nature, whether planting seeds in her garden or wildcrafting herbs to make salves and tinctures, she saw plants as healers. Most famously, she was known for promoting her “onion syrup” cough remedy made with chopped onions and honey.
In 1988, Hana received a pardon from the Czechoslovak government, allowing her to return. Since then, she spent many summers with her family in Prague, travelling back for over three decades. Her last trip was four months before she died.
Hana was delighted with the arrival of successive grandchildren. She was intelligent, compassionate, curious, caring and a generous individual who liked things to be her own way. She liked to end her day with a glass or two of prosecco. When travelling across the country to visit family, she would bring a water bottle filled with wine on the Greyhound bus so she could quietly sip as the sun went down.
Even after her death, Hana is the glue that keeps the family connected. Against her lawyer’s advice she named all four children as co-executors of her estate. All are committed to handling her affairs together as a team - Team Hana.
Jana Razga is Hana Razga’s daughter.
