title: Just like an Italian piazza, this community garden has grown a community
content:
feel good
Just like an Italian piazza, Highbury garden celebrates 30 years of community
Thirty years ago, Mario Minuzzo looked at an overgrown patch of land behind his suburban Adelaide home and saw something special.
"In amongst all of that was vermin and snakes," Mr Minuzzo said.
"The critical thing that started me was when a red-bellied black snake ended up in our house amongst the children on Christmas morning."
Mr Minuzzo sought and was given permission to mow and maintain the land on Aqueduct Reserve at Highbury.
Growing interest from neighbours led to the establishment of the community garden in 1996.
Today, the 88-year-old is celebrating the legacy of the Pioneer Court Community Garden — a place where generations have grown together.
"I recall standing on the mound thirty years ago and thinking this would make a great community garden," Mr Minuzzo said.
"My heritage is Italian and in Italy, local people often meet in the piazza.
"They gather, walk, share stories, and connect, so my original vision for the garden was to create a sense of community and place — just like a piazza."
The community garden is home to more than 40 plots, 75 members and almost 400 fruit and nut trees and vines — from pomegranates and bananas, to grapes and macadamias.
It is on just under one hectare of land leased from the Department for Environment and Water and is one of the larger community gardens scattered across the state.
The garden's 'secret power'
Mr Minuzzo wanted the garden to be somewhere people could meet, share stories and connect.
"Australia in my view is one of the best multicultural examples in the world," he said.
Their membership spans generations, cultures and gardening experience, with long-term members sharing their knowledge with people just starting out.
Chairperson Marina Birch, who took over the reins from Mr Minuzzo in 2022, said she was proud of the garden.
"The secret power of our garden is actually the retired community," she said.
"They keep it going and without them we wouldn't be anywhere.
"But we do have a mix of families with young children, people not quite yet at retirement and a good variety of people from different countries as well."
Laura Fleming is the garden's youngest member.
"It has been so nice to meet local residents and learn from them and grow things I've never grown before," she said.
"It's clearly a huge legacy for Mario and all the people that have been involved.
"It's not been without a lot of hard work and I'm really grateful that they've put this effort in."
A helping hand
The garden's impact also extended beyond its boundaries.
Members grow produce specifically for charity and donate surplus fruit and vegetables to Pathway Community Centre, which partners with OzHarvest to help feed families in need.
The garden members has also been recognised for its contribution to the community, including winning the 2022 City of Tea Tree Gully Australia Day Award for Outstanding Community Group of the Year.
There are already plans for the next chapter, including a proposed native nursery to help restore areas affected by the giant pine scale infestation.

title: Seaman’s Schnapps reaffirms cultural heritage commitment
content:
Seaman’s Schnapps has reaffirmed its commitment to preserving Nigeria’s cultural heritage through its sponsorship of the 2026 Ekimogun Festival in Ondo Kingdom.
The annual festival, also known as the Ogun Festival, celebrates Ogun, the Yoruba deity associated with iron, war and creativity, and attracted traditional rulers, dignitaries, indigenes, tourists and Nigerians in the diaspora.
According to a statement, Seaman’s Schnapps served as the lead sponsor and official prayer drink at the festival, which featured traditional prayers, drumming, carnivals, cultural displays and community competitions.
On the eve of the grand finale, the Seaman’s Schnapps team visited the Osemawe of Ondo Kingdom, Oba Victor Kiladejo, presenting him with an honorarium and a specially commissioned portrait as a gesture of respect for the traditional institution and the Ondo heritage.
The brand also organised an Ayo Olopon competition at Odo Ajomu, drawing participants and spectators while promoting the traditional board game. Its Prayer Hut provided another point of engagement for festival-goers, while a branded media wall showcased its new 20cl product alongside the traditional 3cl offering.
The grand finale featured a cultural troupe supported by Seaman’s Schnapps, which performed traditional dances and eulogies around the Osemawe’s Palace. The brand also supported pounded yam and eating competitions, with winners receiving gifts.
Speaking at the festival, Senior Brand Manager, Nigeria Distilleries Limited, Nnenna Uche-Onyenacho, said the celebration reflected the values associated with the brand.
“The Ogun Festival is a celebration of strength, creativity, and identity, values that are at the very heart of what Seaman’s Schnapps represents as Nigeria’s original prayer drink. We are honoured to stand with the Ekimogun people in preserving and promoting a heritage that belongs not only to Ondo but to all Nigerians,” Uche-Onyenacho said.
She added that the brand’s involvement went beyond commercial visibility and sponsorship.
“Our presence here is not about a logo on a banner. It is about being part of a living culture and helping to preserve and pass it on to future generations,” she said.
Marketing Manager, Nigeria Distilleries Limited, Gbemileke Lawal, said the company’s continued support for the Ekimogun Festival and other cultural celebrations reflected its commitment to treating Nigerian culture as a living expression of national identity.
The Osemawe called on governments at all levels to intensify efforts to preserve indigenous heritage, while urging state and local authorities to support and institutionalise local festivals to boost tourism and cultural development.
The Speaker of the Ondo State House of Assembly, Olamide Oladiji, described the festival as a symbol of the identity and values of the Ondo people, while palace spokesperson, Chief Wole Benson, said Ondo City embraced a carnival atmosphere throughout the celebration.
Seaman’s Schnapps said its continued support for cultural festivals formed part of its broader effort to promote authentic Nigerian culture and encourage younger generations to embrace their heritage.

title: Cherokee youth win legal rights for waterway in first all-female U.S. effort
content:
- On Jan. 8, 2026, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Council unanimously passed a resolution recognizing the inherent legal rights of the Longperson (Ganvhidv Asgaya), an interconnected waterway system whose headwaters rise in the Great Smoky Mountains and end in the sea.
- The resolution was brought forward by the NAIWA Daughters, a group of Indigenous girls aged 10 to 17, making it the first all-female-led rights-of-nature effort in the U.S., and only the second such youth-led resolution passed by a Tribal nation.
- The effort followed 18 months of grassroots organizing and built on the foundations of the rights-of-nature movement, which holds that ecosystems and natural entities should have legal standing to exist and flourish.
- The Longperson resolution grants the waterway five inherent rights and has already spurred related action, including a separate tribal resolution to raise funds for removing the Ela Dam.
Before the proceedings began, the young women carried Longperson into the room with them, water gathered from the mountain headwaters and held in traditional pottery. The chamber filled beyond capacity, supporters spilling into the lobby. When the vote came, the council passed the resolution unanimously. The crowd and the council rose in standing ovation.
On Jan. 8, 2026, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (EBCI) Tribal Council convened in Cherokee, in what is today the U.S. state of North Carolina, to consider a resolution brought forward by the NAIWA Daughters, the youth arm of the North American Indian Women’s Association, made up of a group of Indigenous girls between the ages of 10 and 17.
The resolution recognizes the inherent legal rights of the Longperson, or vwi Ganvhida, the interconnected waterway system whose headwaters rise in the Great Smoky Mountains and travel more than 1,270 kilometers (790 miles), branching through multiple states before its “feet,” as the Cherokee describe it, reach the Gulf of Mexico.
To the Tribe, Longperson (formerly Long Man) is a living entity of great cultural and spiritual significance.
“The room was heavy with the presence of Ancestors and community alike,” said Jasmine Smith, NAIWA Daughters chair and co-founder, describing the moment in a keynote speech at the Bioneers Conference in Berkeley, California. She delivered her speech wearing the moccasins of her Ancestor Ruth Littlejohn.
“That day crystallized in my memories,” she said. “The honor to bring Longperson into the chamber to speak for it, beside it.”
This marks the first all-female-led rights-of-nature effort in the U.S., according to the Earth Law Center, and only the second youth-led rights-of-nature resolution passed by a tribal nation.
“We look to [Longperson] for a lot of strength,” Juanita Wilson, an enrolled EBCI member who has led the Tribe’s annual Honoring Longperson cleanup efforts since 2021 but was not involved with the resolution, told Mongabay. “There are a number of rituals that people do for medicine, physical and emotional health.”
“Whatever’s on land is going to end up in the water,” Wilson added. “It’s literally the lifeblood of everything.”
After the vote, the NAIWA Daughters returned the vessel of water to the Oconaluftee River in a water ceremony.
Rights of Nature movement
The Rights of Nature movement holds that ecosystems and natural entities should have legal standing to exist and flourish, the same way an individual being is endowed with those rights. This framework has been recognized in laws across more than 40 countries. Ecuador added the rights of nature to its Constitution in 2008.
While Indigenous peoples are not universally advocates for the legal rights framework, some have been part of the movement globally, drawing on worldviews that have long considered the natural world as a web of relatives rather than a collection of resources.
In the U.S., many Tribal nations have adopted rights-of-nature legislation. The Ho-Chunk Nation became the first tribal sovereign entity to propose adding the Rights of Nature to its Constitution in 2016, followed by a cascade of resolutions across Indian Country: the Ponca Nation of Oklahoma recognized nature’s right to exist in 2017; the White Earth Band of Ojibwe affirmed the rights of manoomin, or wild rice, to flourish in 2018. The Yurok Tribe established the rights of the Klamath River in 2019. In 2020, the Nez Perce recognized the Snake River as a living entity, and the Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin asserted the Menominee River’s right to remain unpolluted.
Tribes have carried the framework into the courts as well. In 2022, the Sauk-Suiattle Indian Tribe sued the city of Seattle with salmon named as the plaintiff, a case that ended with the city agreeing to build fish passages at its hydroelectric dams.
These efforts — constitutional proposals, resolutions, and lawsuits brought on behalf of rivers, fish, and food sources — form the lineage the NAIWA Daughters have now brought eastward to the Longperson.
“Do we see nature as something we own, or do we view it as something we have the responsibility to protect?” Kyndra Postoak, the group’s Rights of Nature project lead, said in a statement to the EBCI council.
The resolution grants the Longperson five inherent rights: to exist, persist, and regenerate its vital cycles free from harmful human disturbance; to maintain and restore its natural integrity, including freedom from pollution and invasive species; to serve as habitat for nonhuman relatives; to maintain free-flowing conditions; and to be protected under EBCI law and tradition.
“This historic resolution holds a mirror to the Cherokee understanding that the Longperson is a sacred, living relative — not mere property — and translates this relationship into a powerful legal framework,” Grant Wilson, executive director of the Earth Law Center, which supported the effort, told Mongabay in an email. “Those with the deepest cultural and spiritual connections to the land are often the ones best equipped to give Nature a voice in law.”
Old-fashioned organizing
The journey began when the girls were tubing down the river. They noticed tourists staking rocks, which disturbs the habitat for the eastern hellbender salamander (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis alleganiensis, known to the Cherokee as tsuwa). “We were frustrated,” Smith said. “We thought, what if we made a resolution that says you can’t do this?”
Then at the 2024 Indigenous Environmental Network Conference, the NAIWA Daughters met Britt Gondolfi, a lawyer who serves as the Rights of Nature project coordinator for the Bioneers Indigeneity program.
Gondolfi invited them to participate in Bioneers’ six-week rights-of-nature training, introducing the young women to the legal framework that could support their idea. They also connected with other Indigenous communities pursuing similar efforts, including the Mashpee Wampanoag youth, whose 2023 Rights of the Herring resolution had passed their tribal council unanimously.
The NAIWA Daughters initially set out to advocate for protections for the salamanders before elders guided them toward the foundational issue: the waterway itself.
With Bioneers’ support over the following 18 months, Smith said, the NAIWA Daughters were able to focus their efforts on advocating for Longperson. They spent a year and a half hosting community dinners, conducting input surveys, tabling at Cherokee events, and meeting one-on-one with council members to build support.
Smith said the efforts demanded real sacrifice from the young women. “I have watched them give everything to this, showing up tired, overwhelmed, emotional, sacrificing school breaks, weekends, and still fighting for our sovereign rights to be Cherokee,” she said.
“The young women behind this law didn’t AI themselves into this historic moment,” Gondolfi told Mongabay. “They consulted with elders, lawyers, experts in the field, and culture keepers. They put in 18 months of community organizing and created a grassroots movement to honor this ecosystem in law and deed. They revived a traditional customary Indigenous moral philosophy into law.”
“To have feedback from the community say we are 100% behind you,” Smith said, “that’s a win in and of itself, even if the resolution didn’t make it to the floor.”
What comes next
The NAIWA Daughters say their work is far from over. The first Rights of Nature task force meeting took place in May. The task force plans to monitor Longperson’s health, guide further policy implementation, and educate the community as well as other tribal youth.
Within weeks of the passage of the rights-of-nature legislation, the Tribe’s natural resources department and the NAIWA Daughters submitted a resolution committing the EBCI to lead a fundraising campaign to remove the now decommissioned Ela Dam. The resolution passed in March.
For more than a century, the Ela Dam has divided the watershed, blocking the migration path of the critically imperiled sicklefin redhorse (Moxostoma ugidatli). This culturally important fish has been called “the salmon of the south” and its scientific name comes from its Cherokee name meaning “it wears a feather.”
“Just removing the dam will provide safe passage for an aquatic relative,” Kimberly Smith, NAIWA Daughters mentor, told Mongabay.
Smith said removing the dam would also allow sediment buildup at the dam site to be used to create a new Cherokee mound, continuing a cultural practice that stretches back thousands of years.
The NAIWA Daughters plan to present their story at the next national NAIWA convergence in hopes of “inspiring Indigenous women across the country to pursue similar efforts,” Kimberly Smith said.
In the meantime, the annual event Honoring Longperson will take place Sept. 25, during which volunteers and community members clean up the river and NAIWA Daughters plan to hold workshops to teach their younger community members. This year, they also celebrate the success of their rights-of-nature journey.
“Success lives in the groundswell of community and collaboration,” Jasmine Smith said. “We are blessed to live in the oasis of our homelands … we hold the responsibility of stewarding the headwaters, so every living being downstream has water for life.”
New guidebook supports U.S. tribal nations in adopting rights-of-nature laws
Liz Kimbrough is a staff writer for Mongabay and holds a Ph.D. in ecology and evolutionary biology from Tulane University, where she studied the microbiomes of trees. View more of her reporting here.

title: Indu Mitha’s love story carried Bharatanatyam across Partition, kept it alive in Pakistan
content:
The life and times of Bharatanatyam exponent Indu Mitha, who passed away in Dublin at 97 last week after a brief illness, came with numerous twists and turns. The kind that seem as though lifted off a page-turner. Except that Indu’s story isn’t fiction.
In 1951, four years after the bloody Partition, a 22-year-old Indu, daughter of a Bengali-Christian philosophy professor, Gyanesh Chandra Chatterjee, whose family had moved to Delhi from Lahore after Partition, decided to move to Karachi against her parents’ wishes and married a Pakistani army officer, Aboobaker Osman Mitha. The two had met at her uncle’s house party shortly after Partition. A few days later, he saw her again. “I took one look, and my heart turned over… I knew this was the girl I must marry,” wrote Mitha in his memoir years later.
Mitha’s family was as opposed to the match as Indu’s, on grounds of culture and religion, especially amid the divisive space that the Subcontinent had become then. Indu’s older sister, Uma Chatterjee, was married to director Chetan Anand then, which was also not comforting for Mitha’s family, who considered a life around films hardly respectable.
Indu with her husband former Major General of the Pakistani Army, Aboobaker Osman Mitha (Credits: Instagram/ tehreema_mitha)
But despite all odds, Indu crossed over and married Mitha, and the two had three daughters in the following years.
When Indu came to Karachi from Delhi, she brought an unlikely inheritance: Bharatanatyam, the dance form she had imbibed in Delhi and Chennai. Indu had studied philosophy at Delhi University while training in Bharatanatyam under Lalitha Shastry. Shastry was from the first batch of Kalakshetra and had learned under the aegis of Bharatanatyam icon Rukmini Devi Arundale.
Alongside, Indu also studied modern and creative dance with actor and dancer Zohra Sehgal and her husband, Kameshwar Sehgal, at their Zoresh Institute in Lahore while her family still lived there.
Mitha, from a wealthy Bombay family, had joined the British Indian Army in 1942 after graduating from the Indian Military Academy, Dehradun, and served with the Parachute Regiment in Myanmar (Burma then) during the Second World War. After his family moved to Pakistan, Mitha was, in 1954, tasked with setting up the Special Service Group (SSG) of the Army, with help from US Special Forces. He is still known as the ‘Father of the SSG’.
Story continues below this ad
But Bharatanatyam, the art form from Tamil Nadu, was not an obvious choice for a woman making a life in Pakistan, particularly when the country’s cultural ideas became only more conservative with time, mainly in the 1980s. But Indu persisted, and for the next seven decades taught generations of students an art form whose cultural home was far away in the temples and courts of South India — first in Karachi, then in Lahore and later in Islamabad. She taught over 2,000 students. Some of her noted disciples include Amna Mawaz Khan, Iftikhar Masih and her daughter Tehreema, who now runs a dance academy in the US.
“To me, her greatest contribution was teaching young girls in schools in Lahore, who got exposure to Bharatanatyam and later teaching students at her academy, even though there were very few,” says noted Pakistani classical dancer, actor and social activist Sheema Kermani, 75, who was also seen performing classical dance in Ali Sethi’s popular Coke Studio song, Pasoori.
Against all odds
Indu began by teaching dance at Lahore Grammar School and later taught in cantonment houses, schools and academies; performed in drawing rooms and on stages; trained dancers who wanted to and could learn, including her daughter and choreographer Tehreema Mitha. Indu also formed an academy, Mazmoon-e-Shauq, later.
She also experimented with the form’s musical and literary vocabulary, using North Indian instruments and music and setting Urdu poetry to Bharatanatyam, partly because she could not remember all the songs as she was not fluent in Tamil, Telugu and Sanskrit and could not find South Indian orchestras, and partly because she felt that the dance needed to speak to those around her. She translated some of what she remembered into Urdu. This was pioneering work. She was presenting Faiz through Bharatanatyam, rare even in India.
Story continues below this ad
Then came the Zia-ul-Haq years, which were particularly difficult for the arts, especially dance. It was now incompatible with the State’s attempt to define a new Islamic identity. But despite severe odds and many curbs, Indu refused to give up dance and continued to teach. She did so more privately then.
Her daughter’s arangetram in 1986 at the Goethe Institute, as no one else would agree to give them space, took place during the Zia regime. With the organisers providing no help, Indu and Tehreema had to sweep the stage before the performance. Indu contributed to numerous choreographies of Tehreema, including one where a pregnant woman, deserted by her beloved, wants to have the baby.
“This woman’s character is unlike the traditional woman in the classical Bharatanatyam repertoire, who either pines for her lover or portrays her heartbreak… the choreography breaks that mould of traditional Bharatanatyam repertoire and of the female character by raising this unconventional theme and by inherently questioning social mores,” writes Indu’s student Feriyal Aslam in her dissertation Choreographing [in] Pakistan: Indu Mitha, Dancing Occluded Histories in ‘The Land of the Pure’.
‘The spark of an artiste’
Noted Pakistani Kathak dancer Nahid Siddiqui, who trained under Pandit Birju Maharaj in Delhi in the mid-1970s before moving to the UK during General Zia-ul-Haq’s period of martial law, met Mitha in Islamabad at a workshop she conducted at Indu’s academy.
Story continues below this ad
“The spark of an artiste is her life. In a place like Pakistan, where the promotion of classical dance is difficult, and there’s hardly any encouragement, one loses one’s spirit. So, I do think Indu ji felt isolated. But I always saw a sense of calm and peace on her face. She was a very fine woman, always in a sari, and she would almost always attend my performances in Pakistan. But all of us who dance and are from Pakistan have suffered a lot,” Siddiqui, who has been living in exile in London since her popular 13-episode show Payal was taken off the air after six episodes in 1978, says.
But despite this, Indu persevered, teaching those who were willing and making a place for Bharatanatyam in a country where its presence was often complicated.
Bharatanatyam exponent Indu Mitha. (Credits: Instagram/ tehreema_mitha)
Sheema Kermani, one of Pakistan’s most prominent classical dancers and choreographers and the founder of the feminist cultural group Tehrik-e-Niswan, met Indu in 1984 after she returned from India after training at Delhi’s Shriram Bharatiya Kala Kendra, where she learned Bharatanatyam under Leela Samson, Kathak under guru Ram Mohan and Odissi under guru Mayadhar Raut.
“I had just come back to Pakistan and was looking for other dancers in the country. Most dancers (like Siddiqui) had left by then. So, from Karachi, I went to see her in Lahore. I tried to understand how she managed. Indu ji didn’t perform very much and mainly taught. Once I invited her to Karachi to act in a play and she did. When I went to India again in 1988 and came back with more training in Odissi, she was very interested in learning about it,” says Kermani, now 75.
Story continues below this ad
Indu also appeared in the documentary ‘How She Moves’ (2020), which followed her and her students as she prepared for what was intended to be her final recital. Indu, however, later objected to the film, writing that the film represented the filmmaker’s ideas, and not hers.
Mitha was awarded the Presidential Award for Pride of Performance in August 2020 for her exceptional contributions to classical dance and the arts.

title: I ranger aborigeni che stanno ripulendo le coste australiane dalle reti da pesca fantasma
content:
Le spiagge nordoccidentali dell’Australia sono sempre più invase da reti da pesca abbandonate. Le popolazioni aborigene locali si sono organizzate per fare pulizia.


Le popolazioni indigene dell’Australia stanno ripulendo le spiagge da reti da pesca fantasma. Queste intrappolano specie animali come tartarughe e squali, raccolgono rifiuti in acqua trasportandoli fino a riva e una volta qui si sgretolano in microplastiche che restano nell’ambiente per secoli.
Di fronte a questa emergenza, le comunità indigene si stanno organizzando con apposite squadre di ranger che setacciano centinaia di chilometri di costa e ripuliscono l’ambiente. Un lavoro lungo e faticoso, fatto anche con il supporto di strumenti tecnologici come i droni, e che ha assunto una portata internazionale con il coinvolgimento di altri paesi, come l’Indonesia, per prevenire l’abbandono delle reti da pesca.
Reti da pesca e altri rifiuti
Sulle spiagge dell’Australia si stanno accumulando reti da pesca fantasma. Non sono state abbandonate dai pescatori locali, anche perché vengono rinvenute soprattutto in aree protette della Terra di Arnhem o dell’isola di Groote Eylandt, dove l’accesso è riservato esclusivamente alle popolazioni aborigene, che hanno un rispetto di tipo sacro per la loro terra. Provengono piuttosto dal sud-est asiatico, dove vengono abbandonate in mare dai pescatori e trascinate dalle correnti fino alla costa nord-occidentale australiana.


L’Australia ha un grosso problema di rifiuti lungo le proprie spiagge. La situazione più drammatica è quella delle isole e secondo uno studio pubblicato sulla rivista scientifica Nature, solo sulle isole Cocos nel 2019 sono stati rinvenuti un milione di scarpe, 370 mila spazzolini da denti, 414 milioni di oggetti di plastica per un totale di 238 tonnellate di rifiuti. Negli ultimi anni la situazione è migliorata tanto che una ricerca del 2025 dell’agenzia scientifica nazionale australiana ha certificato una riduzione di un terzo dell’inquinamento lungo le sue coste.
Le problematiche rimangono e quello delle reti da pesca è una delle urgenze del presente. In alcuni casi vengono rinvenute come blocchi di plastica dura dopo che qualcuno ha provato a farle sparire bruciandole e fondendole in blocchi. Una volta sulla spiaggia queste reti si sgretolano in microplastiche che impiegano anche secoli per decomporsi. In altri casi intrappolano rifiuti e specie animali marine che vengono poi trascinati fino a riva, sconvolgendo gli ecosistemi e incrementando l’inquinamento.
La missione dei ranger indigeni
La pulizia delle spiagge nordoccidentali dell’Australia dalle reti da pesca fantasma è diventata un’attività sempre più diffusa tra le popolazioni aborigene locali. Squadre di veri e propri ranger ambientali setacciano tratti di costa che si estendono per centinaia di chilometri servendosi di strumentazione di vario tipo. In mare si muovono chiatte con verricelli che individuano le reti da pesca impigliate sui fondali e che vengono così issate in superficie. In cielo invece volano i droni dotati di intelligenza artificiale che individuano le reti dall’alto.
I ranger del popolo aborigeno Anindilyakwa hanno iniziato a lavorare in collaborazione con la Charles Darwin University e l’utilizzo dei droni ha notevolmente semplificato il loro lavoro, visto che è quadruplicato il numero di reti da pesca fantasma individuate. I ranger del popolo Yolŋu, nella penisola di Gove, nel 2025 hanno rimosso circa 13 tonnellate di detriti marini, tra cui numerose reti da pesca.
Raccolta fondi e cooperazione
Nei punti più inquinati delle coste australiane si contano una media di tre tonnellate di detriti per chilometro. E uno dei problemi, quando si trovano le reti da pesca, è cosa farne. Lo spazio nei depositi e nelle discariche è ormai finito e anche quando si trova un buco succede spesso che i gestori le rifiutino per il timore che possano contenere materiali tossici come il piombo. In alcuni casi le reti vengono donate ad artisti locali che le usano per i loro lavori di tessitura ma l’offerta è di gran lunga superiore alla domanda.
A fine 2025 il governo australiano è intervenuto per dare una mano. Sono stati stanziati 25 milioni di dollari per comprare la strumentazione necessaria per pulire le spiagge e sono stati creati nuovi spazi per lo stoccaggio. Una parte dei fondi è stata invece destinata alla prevenzione, coinvolgendo i paesi del sud-est asiatico responsabili dell’abbandono nelle reti da pesca in campagne di sensibilizzazione destinate ai loro pescatori e in sistemi di monitoraggio efficaci. L’obiettivo del governo australiano e delle popolazioni aborigene delle coste nordoccidentali è quello di eliminare completamente le reti fantasma provenienti da fonti internazionali entro il 2030.

title: El rincón más recóndito de Gran Canaria lucha por que no se pierda su Baile de la Papa
content: La Asociación de Vecinos Rosa Nueva ha hecho un trabajo a contrarreloj para rescatar del olvido una tradición de un remoto pueblo de la isla Vivir a la sombra de Inagua y tener Horgazales enfrente ha conformado el carácter de la historia de El Hoyo, un remoto barrio del municipio más recóndito históricamente del resto de los de la isla de Gran Canaria, La Aldea de San Nicolás. Sus vecinos están luchando para poner negro sobre blanco una de las tradiciones más queridas de las Fiestas de San Pedro: el Baile de la Papa. Se trata de una de las manifestaciones coreográficas más singulares del patrimonio inmaterial de la comarca aldeana y, por extensión, de la isla de Gran Canaria. Pero pese a esta relevancia cultural y su presencia constante desde la mitad del pasado siglo, ha sido recientemente cuando la Asociación de Vecinos Rosa Nueva ha impulsado un estudio académico sistemático (ITPCI), con la financiación del Cabildo de Gran Canaria, y que ha llegado a tiempo para recabar los testimonios de los últimos testigos presenciales que lo bailaron o vieron cómo se bailó las primeras veces. Fragmento del mural ubicado en el barrio de El Hoyo en homenaje a su Baile de La Papa. El Baile de la Papa es la historia de personas trabajadoras que en el ocio encontraron espacios de encuentro, identidad y pertenencia. Todas las vecinas entrevistadas consideran El Hoyo, “el barrio más bonito de La Aldea”, aunque reconocen que “toda La Aldea es hermosa y especial”. “El truco está en no dejarse mover la papa” El Baile de la Papa, que no obedece ni a la fecha de su cosecha, ni tiene un arraigo religioso, ni aborigen, ha subsistido sin interrupción, salvo el año de la pandemia, por la plena voluntad de los vecinos de El Hoyo de divertirse y de que no desaparezca. Fue traído al barrio por Jorge Ojeda Montesdeoca, que pudo verlo en otros pueblos en fiestas donde ya se interpretaba el baile, recogido, tal vez, en la película que se proyectó en aquella época Serenata en el Valle del Sol (Duches of Idaho), de Robert Z. Leonard, un film en el que tiene lugar el Potato Dance, una competición al estilo de la realizada en El Hoyo, sujetando la papa con la frente, con las manos en la espalda, y aumentando la dificultad del baile a medida que se intensifica la música de la orquesta o del grupo que esté sobre el escenario. “El truco está en no dejarse mover la papa”, cuenta a esta redacción Gabriel Ramírez, que ha ganado hasta en cuatro ocasiones en esta competición, siempre con la misma pareja, su esposa Margarita González. Ella recuerda a sus 85 años cómo las fiestas de San Pedro se hacían antes de tener la talla del santo, cómo fue con otras dos niñas pidiendo para comprarla, cómo la trajeron al hombro a El Hoyo y cómo, años después, llegó El Baile de la Papa. Gabriel Ramírez sostiene a un niño en brazos junto a sus vecinos de El Hoyo en las fiestas de San Pedro. Años 60. Para ella, la mejor estrategia es mover la cintura y dejar quieta la papa en la frente, “la cabeza quietita”. Margarita no quiere que esta tradición se pierda y le da esperanza cómo los jóvenes se animan a bailarla en cada edición desde hace casi 70 años. Una parranda que empezó en un garaje Teresa Cárdenes tiene 83 años y en El Hoyo todo el mundo la conoce por Teresita. Llegó en 1959 desde Tejeda cuando tenía 16 años. Teresa Cárdenes Quintana, Nicolasa Ojeda Suárez, Carmen Ramírez, Margarita González Suárez, Gabriel Ramírez Montesdeoca y Ana María Díaz Suárez, vecinas y vecino de El Hoyo entrevistados para este reportaje. En su casa todos son amantes de la música y ella toca “la laúd” (sic). “Cantaba de chica en medio de los tomateros, pero ya no”. No es de extrañar que Jorge fuera su cuñado. Y ella recuerda cómo fue: “Él, un día que se cogieron las papas en El Hoyo, cogió un balde con las papas todas del mismo tamaño y el baile se hacía en el garaje de mi casa”, cuenta Teresita. “Los asientos eran cajas de tomates para que las madres pudieran vigilar si las hijas se pegaban mucho a las parejas”. Esta vecina recuerda que la introducción del baile no estuvo exenta de polémica y que algunas personas mayores del pueblo “acusaron a Jorge de inventar este baile para arrimarse más a las mujeres” (ríe). A la sombra del almácigo Nico Ojeda, de 76 años, recuerda aquellos momentos en que había fiesta antes que santo, ya que fue una de las tres niñas que fue pidiendo casa por casa. “Venía gente andando de todas partes, de Tasarte, Tasartico, desde por la mañana para la fiesta del mediodía y comían a la sombra del almácico (sic), almuerzo, merienda, bailes de taifas y después se iban a su casa”. Los vecinos de El Hoyo llevan a hombros a San Pedro en las fiestas.Año 1959. “Todo el que quería bailar la papa, la podía bailar. Se ponían enfrente, no se podía rodar la papa para el ojo, si se rodaba para el ojo te descalificaban”, explica la vecina. Había un jurado conformado por personas del barrio y de otros sitios, y si la papa se movía o se sujetaba con la nariz, tampoco valía. Luego se iba incrementando la dificultad: se bailaba a la pata coja, con las manos atrás, con las manos arriba, según la música se fuera acelerando, y después la pareja ganadora recibía un trofeo. “Había parejas que eran de la misma altura, que estaban acostumbrados a bailar juntos, más o menos la pareja se elegía pensando en todo eso”. La labor de la Asociación de Vecinos Rosa Nueva Begoña Saavedra, presidenta de la Asociación Rosa Nueva nos atiende en El Hoyo para contarnos cómo nació la inquietud de reactivar la labor que comenzaron hace 48 años los vecinos del barrio.“Mi padre fue uno de los constructores y socios fundadores, pensé que si teníamos el espacio y la asociación por qué no reactivarlo para todos y crear participación ciudadana, un sitio de encuentro, para recopilar costumbres, tradiciones de la zona, algo que nos parece muy importante para saber de dónde venimos”. Begoña Saavedra Ramírez, presidenta de la Asociación de Vecinos Rosa Nueva y vecina de El Hoyo. Begoña, auxiliar de vuelo, el tiempo que no está en el aire está en su barrio, del que ha aprendido que la distancia no es algo realmente importante, si la gente tiene realmente ganas de comunicarse. “Nos dimos cuenta de que la gente se nos acercaba cuando creábamos el espacio, empezando por actividades para los niños que implicaban a los padres, las clases de costura, pero había muchas ganas de compartir mucha información que todo el mundo guardaba y tenían necesidad de hablar y de hablar del pasado”. Fue en uno de esos encuentros, cocinados a fuego lento y con la espera adecuada, entre café y un poquito de agua guisada, donde se propuso que se hiciera algo por salvaguardar y difundir el baile. “El Baile de la Papa era uno de los puntos recurrentes en la memoria de los socios aunque sin datos muy claros, y, dado que tampoco existía información documentada, desde la asociación vimos la urgencia de comenzar a investigarlo para documentarlo; los motivos por los que este baile empezó aquí, en El Hoyo”. Primer estudio académico patrimonial Fue entonces cuando, en la búsqueda de financiación, dieron con la subvención de la Reserva de la Biosfera y Patrimonio Mundial, enclave en el que se encuentra El Hoyo. “Solo tener las conclusiones del estudio patrimonial en las manos ya fue un triunfo. Nosotras, desde la Junta Directiva, intuíamos que teníamos algo grande entre las manos aunque no viniera de los antiguos canarios, pero es algo que se ha hecho anualmente desde 1959 en un lugar remoto como este, de una determinada manera”. En el centro. Begoña Saavedra Ramírez, presidenta de la Asociación Rosa Nueva; junto a Guadalupe, miembro de la Junta Directiva; y la socia y profesora de costura, Mercedes, a la izquierda. Con el estudio en la mano, se ha solicitado que el Baile de la Papa sea considerado Bien de Interés Cultural Inmaterial a nivel autonómico o insular y la asociación continúa con su proceso de difusión y visibilización en colegios y centros culturales. “El Baile de la Papa tiene una amenaza”, advierte Begoña. “La principal es que no podamos recoger todo lo que las personas mayores puedan decirnos antes de que se vayan y también necesitamos implicar a las generaciones nuevas y por eso es fundamental que se conozca y que se interesen por él desde todas partes”. Para Guadalupe Godoy, miembro de la Junta Directiva, es fundamental que se difunda “tal y como se bailó en 1959, que no se pervierta”. “Un renacer” En conversaciones con este periódico, usuarias de la Asociación cuentan lo que ha significado para ellas tener un punto de encuentro en el barrio. “Las mujeres en el barrio no teníamos nada, ahora tenemos un sitio donde coser, donde tomarnos el buchito de café y recuperar las cosas de antes”, confiesa Carmen Ramírez. “Después de toda una vida de trabajos en la agricultura, el almacén de tomates, trabajar en el sur, tener hijos... ahora es mi tiempo”. Un grupo de vecinos viendo fotos en la Asociación Rosa Nueva. Nicolasa Ojeda explica la importancia de compartir en comunidad y salir del individualismo. “Los vecinos nos cuidamos y nos acompañamos porque eso es un paño que se pone en toda mesa, si no ayudamos a los demás, los demás no nos pueden ayudar cuando los necesitemos”. O Ana María Díaz Suárez, de 70 años, que explica cómo esto para ella ha sido “un renacer”. La profesora de costura Mercedes Hernández, jubilada de la docencia, aunque de eso una nunca se jubila, llegó a El Hoyo a dar clases de forma altruista y se enamoró de su gente y su paisaje. “Ya casi soy aldeana”, asegura. “Vienen muchas señoras que están jubiladas, hablamos, aprendemos y como todas se conocen es como una familia: ellas salen de casa y yo encantada”.

title: Luo Yang’s Diaspora Birds Lands in NYC Chinatown
content:
Karen Wong steps into Manhattan’s Chinatown with Luo Yang, meeting the seven women behind her latest Diaspora Birds series
When Luo Yang was in her twenties, she began capturing a new generation of young women, her generation, of lived experience in China. Traveling across the continent, she sought out communities where young people were discovering their voices and individuality. Following the visual diaristic lineage of Nan Goldin and Ryan McGinley, Luo establishes trust and elicits an intimate connection with her subjects; many became friends, whom she documented over two decades in her best-known series, Girls.
In 2012, artist and dissident Ai Weiwei praised Yang as one of the “rising stars of Chinese photography”. He included her in his group exhibition of 37 contemporary Chinese artists, “Fuck Off 2,” presented in 2013 at the Groningen Museum in the Netherlands. As her profile grew in Europe, she was accepted to the Cité internationale des Arts 2022 artistic residency program in Paris. While in the city of lights, she encountered her first Chinatown. She shares, “Chinatown was familiar, but it felt like China from a different era, frozen in time; immigrants from an older generation brought an aesthetic that China has moved on from.” Visiting various European cities, Yang met Asian women who resettled in the West and whose stories of shifting cultural identities spurred her latest ongoing portrait series, Diaspora Birds.
In May this year, Yang was on assignment in New York City and was commissioned to extend her Diaspora Birds project to include a group of New Yorkers born in Asia. While scouting for locations, she chose Manhattan’s Chinatown as the obvious backdrop and shot all seven women in one long day. It’s no coincidence that, having recently turned 40, Yang is capturing the stories of accomplished, creative women in the prime of their lives.
With a sensitive eye and calm demeanour, Yang read the energy of each woman and set them up in a restaurant, barbershop, gift shop, or next to a fruit vendor. She was looking for that elevated moment, where there was a bit more drama, possibility, and imagination. After wrapping up the photoshoot, Yang, besotted with her new friends, whom she described as “so beautiful,” felt more connected than ever to the city of New York.
Presented as an Elephant exclusive:
LUO YANG
Diaspora Birds (Manhattan Chinatown), 2026.
FiFi Zhang is a Shanghai-born, NYC-based electronic producer, vocalist, DJ, and visual artist. Signed songwriter at 88rising, her self-produced debut album, FLEETING HEARTS, earned Best Electronic Album at the 2025 HMA Awards.
“Chinatown feels like a time capsule of my homeland, China, with its traditional Cantonese restaurants, newly opened bubble tea shops, fashion boutiques, and the lingering scent of the fish markets. I love playing table tennis in Chinatown, walking along Allen Street, and ending my day with a great meal at August Gatherings.”
Yuhee Yang is a dancer, choreographer, and movement director originally from Jeju Island, South Korea.
“Chinatown is where I go to ground myself and recharge. The chaotic, vibrant energy of the neighbourhood always makes me feel inspired and connected to New York.”
Shien Lee was born in Taiwan and currently resides in Brooklyn. She is the founder of the Red Pavilion in Bushwick, a beacon of AAPI culture and resilience.
“I surround myself with incredible Asian female artists through my club, and I was actually brought on to the project through another Chinese female photographer that shot our opening party – so being chosen by Luo Yang to work on this project felt especially special.”
Ruoyi Jiang is the founder of NYC Chinatown boutique Chop Suey Club. Born in Beijing, she was a professional golfer and scuba diving instructor before earning her BFA in photography from NYU. She is a leading voice in Mahjong culture and the author of Mahjong For Dummies.
“I was a fan of Luo Yang already, so I was really excited to meet her and be photographed by her! Our store actually carried her photo book, Girls, when it first came out. I love her perspective on Asian femininity, she understands how strength and individuality manifest in Asian women.”
Natasha Jen is an award-winning designer, educator, and partner at Pentagram.
“NYC’s Chinatown is messy, crowded, imperfect, and comforting. It reminds me of Taipei. They share a certain density, directness, and sense of everyday life happening all at once. I go there when I want something specific to eat, but also when I want to feel briefly closer to home.”
Jacky Lee was born in South Korea in 1957, she was relinquished by her Korean mother at age five alongside her younger sister and adopted by a Black military family.
“As a biracial adoptee, being photographed by an Asian woman was really meaningful. I felt embraced.”
Bea was raised in Flushing, Queens. Ever since she was little, she was interested in creating, from drawing to crafting to gardening with her grandparents.
“I worked at a boutique in Chinatown for almost 10 years, and it’s how I met and made most of my best friends today.”

title: Elder among last to remember Australia's forgotten 'parkland'
content:
Aunty Carol Pettersen recalls Western Australia's farming landscape before mass clearing
Menang Elder Aunty Carol Petterson was four years old when her family worked as shepherds.
They would drive the herd through bushland and along rivers towards the West Australian coast.
Standing on the same rocks they once used to cross the Gairdner River, about 200 kilometres south-east of Perth, she has vivid memories of the landscape.
"There were no fences around … it was like a parkland," she said.
"I can still visualise it."
The family didn't have dogs; they drove the sheep themselves, and so long as the lead sheep was headed in the right direction, the rest would follow.
"I had a wonderful childhood," she said.
"We didn't have motor cars, and I almost feel like I'm from the dinosaur era because we walked."
And walk they did, managing up to 20 kilometres a day, keeping pace with the horse and cart carrying their gear.
Back then, places were known only by their Noongar names.
Nearby Jerramungup was Yarramoup, "up" meaning "place" of the "tall" (yarra), "yate" trees (mo).
Aunty Carol said it was the only place around where yate trees grew on a hill.
"So when the people said Yarramoup, you knew where to go because we'd follow the hills and the landmarks to know where we were going," she said.
They learned to read the country around them.
"We knew about the weather, we knew about the animals, we knew where the bush foods were," she said.
"If there was samphire by the creek, we would wrap it up in paperbark with meat and put it on the coals.
"We gathered our salt from the bush and our sweetness from honey.
"To this day, I don't use sugar, and very little salt."
For Aunty Carol, country provided everything they needed.
"It's home," she said.
"When you look at the bush, it's our kitchen, it's our dining room, it's our yarning room, it's our classroom, it's our study area, it's our therapeutic area."
But the country Aunty Carol remembers was a much richer and more abundant landscape than the one seen today.
Gondwana Link chief executive Keith Bradby has studied early explorer journals to understand just how dramatically the landscape and its wildlife have changed.
"I've read the early explorer journals, trying to understand how different the country was then, because there's no question it was very different," he said.
"You had people like James Drummond, who went through that country in the 1840s, just marvelling at its botanical richness.
"If you read the early journals, the big hazard of riding through the bush was that woylies and tammars would just bolt out all the time and startle the horses."
An excerpt from surveyor John Septimus Roe's journal, dated October 22, 1848, described it as "a large extent of good grassy country … well watered by a river and its numerous branches".
But by 1950, the Hassell Estate was sold to the state government and mass clearing began to make way for post-war soldier resettlement.
Aunty Carol and her siblings are among the last to remember what it was like before that time.
She hopes her story will inspire people to reconnect with country.
"We don't see any separation, everything is whole," she said.
"Everything is connected, and we are only just one little part of that."

title: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government
content: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government tia.roberts Tue, 09/15/2026 - 11:14 CSQ Issue 50-3. Cultural Sovereignty: Self-Determination Through Indigenous Governance September 2026 Read on Issuu Buy a copy Subscribe Gunayala is a leading example of Indigenous autonomy and self-government in Abya Yala. The Guna Peoples have been defending their territory, their identity, and their own form of governance long before international instruments such as the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples formally recognized the rights to self-determination, autonomy, and self-government. Our Peoples have been practicing their own forms of organization and decision-making for centuries, and today we continue to live and exercise these internationally recognized rights in Gunayala. The ancestral territory of Gunayala Comarca is located on the Caribbean coast of Panama and extends to the Colombian border, comprising mainland, forests, rivers, mangroves, coastlines, the sea, and numerous islands where our communities are located. It is the home of our Guna ancestors, and is where we continue to live and pass on our knowledge and our way of understanding the world. Its coastline is approximately 315 kilometers long and includes more than 400 small islands and islets; we often describe our communities as seaside villages. Our people traverse this territory from the mountain ranges, down its rivers, through the forests, mangroves, and beaches until we reach the sea, the islands, the coral reefs, and the white sands—places that are not only part of our geography, but also our memory, our spirituality, and our struggles. Our autonomy did not originate from a State law, and our form of self-governance existed long before its formal legal recognition. Law 16, enacted on February 19, 1953, legally organized what was then called the Comarca of San Blas, now Gunayala. Subsequently, other laws and judicial decisions have recognized our organization and autonomy. Fully understanding our autonomy also requires remembering an event that profoundly marked our history: the Dule Revolution of 1925. The Dule, or People’s, Revolution was a decisive moment in the defense of our rights, our territory, our culture, and our way of life against the Panamanian government’s policies that sought to “civilize the Indians of San Blas,” as our people were then known. In truth, we already had our own civilization, with authorities, norms, knowledge, spirituality, and a worldview that guided our lives long before the Republic of Panama existed. The Revolution did not create our autonomy, but rather defended and reaffirmed it. This year, as we commemorate 101 years since that feat, it continues to hold profound meaning for us. The autonomy that our ancestors defended more than a century ago does not belong only to the past; it endures and is exercised every day in our communities. One of the spaces where our form of self-governance comes to life is the Onmagged Nega, the House of Congress, where the community gathers to listen, dialogue, and reflect on the issues that affect us, and to make collective decisions. There, our Sagla (traditional authorities) guide us through their songs, which transmit the memory, knowledge, and teachings of our ancestors, while the Argar help interpret that knowledge and relate it to the situations the community experiences in the present. Murals in Gunayala reflect the Guna way of life, which bridges land and sea. Photo by Julien Defourny. For us, song is not separate from governance. In our worldview, governing means not only managing resources, approving laws, or exercising authority, but also guiding, listening, advising, transmitting knowledge, and assuming responsibility toward the community. From each of our communities, a broader collective structure is built that connects the 49 communities of Gunayala through the Guna General Congress, where our people have organized to govern themselves collectively. The Congress is our highest political and administrative body and addresses matters related to territory, natural resources, education, and other issues that affect the lives of our communities, as well as maintaining relations with the State and other institutions. Alongside it is the General Congress of Guna Culture, responsible for strengthening our Traditional Knowledge, spirituality, songs, language, and other cultural expressions that form our identity. This relationship between the two institutions demonstrates a fundamental tenet of our model: governance, culture, spirituality, knowledge, and territory are not separate, but interconnected. Decisions in Gunayala are made collectively, guided by our customary law, norms, and worldview. The Igardummadwala, our Fundamental Law—together with the statutes, regulations, and resolutions from our Congresses, as well as community norms—forms our unique system and expresses our right to govern ourselves according to our own rules and institutions. This takes on special importance in the face of external projects or interests, because self-government cannot be reduced to mere recognition written in a law. It only becomes real in practice when a Peoples can make decisions about matters that transform their territory and way of life. Maraca with a Naa Ukuryaa. This symbol has been part of Guna culture for centuries, representing the octopus that created the universe, the four cardinal points, and the origin point of humanity. Photo by Julien Defourny. Over time, our autonomy has been tested by various interests in our territory and resources, and in recent years, by proposals for development megaprojects such as the Central America Electrical Interconnection System. In the face of these situations, our authorities, assemblies, resolutions, and internal norms serve as tools for exercising our autonomy. Governing ourselves means having the ability to say no, to set conditions, and to decide what is compatible with our vision for our territory. To see Gunayala as a model of self-government does not imply it is a perfect system, or one frozen in time. Our self-government is a living system that must continue to adapt to the challenges of today. Some of our practices and forms of knowledge have weakened over time, and many of our young people live outside the territory. Our communities are undergoing social, economic, cultural, and environmental transformations, while climate change increasingly impacts our coasts, islands, and ecosystems. Maintaining our autonomy entails acknowledging these realities and continuing to strengthen our heritage so that our language, knowledge, norms, and unique forms of organization remain meaningful for future generations. I am proud to note that in 2017, I helped found what is now known as the General Congress of Guna Youth—a space dedicated to strengthening our people’s leadership, conservation efforts, and values in Gunayala. We also cannot overlook the young people living outside the territory who maintain ties to their communities and return to visit their families, participate in traditional ceremonies, celebrate community anniversaries, or commemorate the Guna Revolution. This relationship with new generations is fundamental to ensuring that our culture, knowledge, and self-governance continue to strengthen over time. Women also play a vital role in this continuity, as they participate in passing on our language, knowledge, and cultural practices, and in shaping new generations. Likewise, our relationship with the land is expressed through knowledge systems like Nainu, our traditional agricultural practice. Passed down through generations and rooted in an understanding of cycles, crops, and land management, it reminds us that our way of governing ourselves is deeply intertwined with how we care for life. In the face of biodiversity loss and climate change, Gunayala’s experience has much to offer—not because we hold all the answers, but because over generations, we have learned that there can be no autonomy without territory, no territory without knowledge, and no knowledge without community. Our experience demonstrates that recognizing the rights of Indigenous Peoples means more than simply outlining a territory on a map. It requires respecting their authorities, institutions, knowledge systems, and norms, and, above all, their capacity to make collective decisions about their present and future. Our autonomy is not merely a right recognized by laws or international instruments. It is a practice we continue to exercise, defend, and strengthen through the Onmagged Nega, our Congresses, our norms, the transmission of our knowledge, and the defense of the territory inherited from our ancestors. Perhaps one of the greatest contributions Gunayala can share with other Indigenous Peoples and the world is demonstrating that self-governance is not a relic of the past, but a living expression of our self-determination and a collective commitment to safeguarding who we are, our territory, and the legacy we will leave to future generations. --Iniquilipi Chiari-Lombardo (Guna) is Deputy Secretary of the Guna General Congress. May Pérez (Guna) is Cultural Survival Panama Advocacy Coordinator. Top photo: Uggubseni community in the Gunayala Comarca in Panama. Photo by Iniquilipi Chiari-Lombardo/TV Indígena. Main Image
